LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by my hon. friend from York South, to move the adjournment of the house under standing order No. 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the extensive lay-offs of railway employees and others which are causing widespread hardship and insecurity for thousands of Canadians.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It would be helpful to hear the hon. member on the question of urgency of debate.

maintopic: LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I wish to make three points. The first is that there is no other opportunity to raise this critical matter, in view of the fact that the estimates for the present fiscal year have already been passed. It is true there is a supply motion yet to be called but we have no notice from the government as to when it will be called. This is the only way this matter can be discussed, and we think it is important that it should be discussed.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m)
Second, I want to point out that this is a matter of national importance in that it affects almost every area of Canada. Some 4,000 railway employees have already been laid off. Many of these may be permanent lay-offs. In some circles it is thought that lay-offs may reach 10,000 before the spring. The distribution of the lay-offs to date by the Canadian National Railways alone has been 450 men in the Atlantic region, 460 in the St. Lawrence area, 500 in the Winnipeg-lakehead-Saskatchewan area, 640 in British Columbia and 640 in Ontario. Therefore it is seen that this problem spreads from coast to coast and is not merely a local one.
The third point I want to make is that this is a matter of great urgency. Four thousand men laid off on four days notice involves a great deal of hardship for those men and
their families and a considerable dislocation of the economy of the communities in which they live. I want to point out it is an urgent matter. It seems to me that at this time the House of Commons, the people of Canada and particularly the men involved have a right to know what steps the government intends taking to cope with this problem, whether any legislation is in contemplation, and what programs the government has in mind to prevent further lay-offs and to provide employment for the men already laid off. It seems to me this matter cannot be delayed, it ought to be discussed, and it should be discussed today because it is of the utmost importance not only to the people involved but to the Canadian economy generally.

maintopic: LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to support this adjournment motion. I think the subject is national in scope and in the last few days has taken on extreme urgency. I agree that there does not appear to be any other opportunity to discuss this matter now that the estimates of the Department of Transport are out of the way, and there does not seem to be any proposed legislation on which a discussion could take place.
I notice, as recorded in Hansard for October 30, that in answer to a question from the hon. member for Halifax the Minister of Transport promised that some statement would be made on freight rate increases. We are still waiting for it; in fact many of us expected that some sort of announcement would be made today. The minister himself has admitted that one reason for these layoffs has been the increases in freight rates.
For some strange reason the lay-offs started in the maritimes. It is the same old story, but now they have spread across the country. Some 500 men have been laid off in Winnipeg, and I know there are rumours out there of even greater lay-offs. The matter is urgent. It needs some attention. In reply to a question in the house the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said he felt that the notice given employees was not sufficient, and we know there is an argument as to whether the agreements between the unions and the railways insist on a 90 day notice.

speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member at this time. He must only deal with the necessity of adjourning the regular business of the house to discuss, not any other matter, but the definite matter referred to in the motion of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.

maintopic: LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I thank Your Honour for this information and I shall restrict my remarks to the terms of the motion.
I simply wanted to draw a parallel between the urgency of this matter and that of other economic situations in our country related to precisely the same state of affairs. Even if we were to discuss these lay-offs all afternoon, it would not give work to C.N.R. employees tomorrow morning.
These people are suffering the consequences of an obsolete economic system

that applies not only to them but to the whole population. That is why I say it is not so urgent to discuss the question of the railroad employees because we will not solve it this afternoon, but we should face the whole economic questions in Canada and let the government or the Department of Transport discuss with the authorities of the C.N.R. anything relevant to this particular case so as to find the means to restore order in the economic field.
So, I do not believe that the urgency is as pressing as the motion now before us suggests.

maintopic: LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we are confronted with this same matter of urgency of debate. I imagine the first question we must consider, and which I hope Your Honour is considering in respect of your ruling, is when would we have otherwise an opportunity to discuss this very serious national problem. The leader of the New Democratic party has dealt with the lay-offs on the railways and has shown that this is not a problem which is local in nature but is one which exists across the country. There have been 800 lay-offs in the city of Calgary alone. This is a matter which is national in scope and I ask, when can we discuss it. I think we must take into consideration the fact that because of the new rules and the guillotine method many questions remain unanswered; opposition and other members of parliament are unable to obtain answers from the minister.
I support the motion of the leader of the New Democratic party in this regard and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you should allow this debate. Not only is this matter national in scope, it is also all wrapped up in the problems in respect of the loss of the coal markets, the loss of the wheat markets, the high freight rates and so on. All these things are interrelated with the lay-offs. The railway companies have no work because there are no wheat or coal markets. This in turn can also be related to the comparative cost of transporting coal in Canada and in the United States. One cannot isolate these things. We have not had the opportunity of obtaining answers from the government because of the new rules.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a parallel which may well have occurred to Your Honour and which I should like to draw to Your Honour's attention in connection with the motion now before us. Mr. Speaker, I was hesitating because I thought the Minister of National Health and Welfare was going to speak. I will yield to him and speak later if he wishes to speak now. Since the government house leader does not accept my offer to speak before I do, I will refute his arguments before he advances them.
It is quite clear that what we have to concern ourselves about is urgency of debate. In addition to the rules and precedents we have in Beauchesne's fourth edition and in other places we now have a very useful supplement in the form of an article on this question which was written by Hon. Lucien Lamoureux, M.P., Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada. It appeared in the July issue of "The Parliamentarian" which is the journal of the parliaments of the Commonwealth. I dearly wish I had time to put the whole article on the record because it would be useful to do so; then it would be translated into French as well. May I read two or
Lay-Offs of Railway and Other Employees three sentences for Your Honour's guidance. First may I agree, as I am sure Your Honour will, with the opening sentence of the article, which reads:
The decision as to whether or not a motion to adjourn the house should be allowed for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance is one which taxes the judgment of the Speaker to the utmost.
Having said that, Your Honour in this article got around to the specific matters which have to be weighed in arriving at this decision, and you then said this about the Speaker:
He must be satisfied that the matter raised is one of genuine urgency and that no other opportunity for raising it would occur in the normal course of parliamentary business.
I suggest that is a very clear statement, and that this motion meets both those conditions; it deals with a matter of genuine urgency, and there is no foreseeable opportunity for discussing it in the normal course of parliamentary business. Later in the same article Your Honour said this:
Urgency alone is not sufficient to qualify an emergency adjournment motion for acceptance. The matter must be one of overriding national urgency and not merely of regional urgency-
It has been clearly demonstrated that this is an issue of concern not only to one region or another but that it is one of national urgency. Then, Mr. Speaker, in an excellent concluding paragraph to this article you said:
In these days of heavy parliamentary pressure an emergency procedure is essential to ensure that an opportunity for debating a genuinely urgent and sudden crisis can always be found. The Speaker has an important duty to ensure that the procedure is not abused-
Speaking from the opposition side, I agree.
-but it is equally important that he should protect the right of the private member to secure an emergency debate when the circumstances justify it, no matter how pressing the demands of government business may be.
I suggest that the motion presented today meets the criteria which Your Honour has laid down. This is an urgent question, it is one of national importance, there is no immediate opportunity to deal with it, and it is the type of question for which this kind of motion is provided.
Let me give some examples of the kind of thing we ought to be able to find out; namely, to what extent are these lay-offs seasonal, to what extent are they caused by technological change, and what are the steps we should be taking to deal with them? I submit this is the kind of information that could

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: LAY-OFFS OF RAILWAY AND OTHER EMPLOYEES-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I thank hon. members for their contribution to this interesting discussion, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I would remind the hon. member that the words he has quoted were spoken ex cathedra and therefore I do not feel bound by such obiter dicta. I feel that a much better authority is Beauchesne's fourth edition. Perhaps hon. members would allow me to refer to citation 100, which is well known and has been quoted in circumstances such as these. This citation has been referred to by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam. Citation 100 says:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough-
As has been said before, "early enough" is an absolutely relative term. One may ask how early is "early enough"? It has been mentioned that although the estimates have been completed there is to be a supply debate before the 27th of this month, that is within the next 19 days. Of course this is the outside limit, and debate on this motion might be had before that time by arrangement. In any event, it would definitely be brought before the house by that date. I have some doubts, therefore, whether the motion qualifies in view of this situation. I would also remind hon. members of paragraph 8 of citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition wherein a former Speaker is quoted as having said:
I do not think that, under the standing order of 1882, a motion on a subject of this kind, having such a very wide scope, was ever contemplated. What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs. But I do not think it was contemplated-if the house will allow me to state my views-that a question of very wide scope, which would demand legislation to deal with it in any effective manner, should be the subject of discussion on a motion for the adjournment of the house.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I would think this citation covers the situation. For the guidance of hon. members I should like to refer them to an even more eminent authority, and quote from a ruling made by Mr. Speaker in the year 1961 following an adjournment motion proposed by

DEBATES	November 7. 1967
the then hon. member for Laurier. This motion had reference to a matter of definite urgent public importance, namely the displacement of C.N.R. employees. I am reading from Hansard of March 13, 1961 at page 2907. The Speaker then said:
As hon. members will recall, the matter of layoffs of employees of the Canadian National Railways arises very frequently during the question period, and the minister is always under the necessity of having to say that he will inquire from the C.N.R. to find out what their policy is and that he will bring back an answer to the house. It seems to me that citation 100, which indicates that such matters should relate to the administrative responsibility of the government, might be applied in this case in the sense that the responsibility is indirectly through parliament and not one on which a debate on a motion of this kind could have any direct effect or result. It would be necessary for parliament to amend its Canadian National Railways legislation, if an enforceable decision is to be made or an effective remedy applied.
The Speaker concluded that he had to refuse the hon. member leave to make the motion.
In view of this precedent and in view of the citations I have quoted I do not think it is possible for me to accept the motion advanced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.

IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY The house resumed, from Monday, November 6, consideration of the motion of Miss LaMarsh for the second reading of Bill No. C-163, to implement a broadcasting policy for 
Canada, to amend the Radio Act in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential and related provisions.

Last night before ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was discussing the responsibility of this house to Canadian parents and families in providing through Bill C-163 a vehicle which will bring broadcasting, both public and private, under adequate and effective control so as to assure families and parents that television programming will be of a type that will strengthen the family unit, encourage character building and inspire the nation to build a clean, strong and free society in which there is respect for integrity, law and authority.
The petition of 80,000 women presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and to members of this house a few years ago stated that the true function of the C.B.C. should be to help raise a generation with strength, character and the courageous leadership that the opportunities of this age demand. I stated that while many C.B.C. programs are commendable, such as the very positive and constructive job of portraying the best of our centennial celebrations, many others are rotten trash which undermine the family, the faith and morality of the home, and degrade human character. I also referred to the fact that all too often a small, misguided minority, usually producers, carry on this type of activity in defiance of management and government policy. Therefore the legislation that we are considering must have teeth in it to stop and control this type of thing. The taxpayers who subsidize this multimillion dollar industry must have some say in the affairs of their public broadcasting facility.
A good example of what I am referring to, Mr. Speaker, was the program last Sunday night between ten and eleven o'clock on abortion, produced by Patrick Watson. To say the least, in the setting that it was aired this film was pornography at its worst, pure unadulterated evil watched by millions of families, by children, and by young girls serving as babysitters. Was this a program for young girls? Was it not possible to discuss the controversial issue of legalized abortion in a rational and reasonable way without showing everything, including the screaming of a hysterical girl undergoing an abortion operation?
Another point in question concerns national unity. The Prime Minister has said this is our most vital and urgent problem. Yet last night a great deal of time was given to Rene Levesque and his radical separatist views
November 7, 1967

uttered in Toronto on the week end. No mention was made of the spectacular world week end in Edmonton, nor was there mention of the remarkable reception given the Governor General by his local townspeople, boyhood friends and schoolmates in Red Deer and Lacombe. Neither was there mention made in prelude of the centennial celebration of parliament which took place yesterday.
The public demand for more effective control of broadcasting is not only from parents, from taxpayers and from the elected representatives of the people, including the majority of the members of this house. It is shared by every aspect of Canadian life, including the press. The following quotations from the press, which I have kept down through the months, are just a sample of public opinion as recorded in the English press regarding the C.B.C., beginning three years ago when the government at last took action which has resulted in the present legislation. I may add that the French press has been just as outspoken and just as firm. The Vancouver Province, on October 30, 1964, said:
Now that the Pearson government admits its responsibility from the C.B.C., the taxpayer can look to Ottawa to rescue the C.B.C. from the curious crew that seem to have taken over so many C.B.C. productions-
The odd crew took over because C.B.C. management abdicated its responsibility to direct and control-
Before the C.B.C. drifts any further into the strange experiments of some of its employees, before it becomes regarded solely as a profitable hang-out for wispy bearded beatniks, impersonating genuinely creative talent, the government will have to get busy and put the C.B.C.'s house in order.
The Calgary Herald on October 29, 1964, said:
There is little doubt that, on occasion, some of the "far-out" employees of the public broadcasting system in Canada have been misusing the tremendous power given them. There have been quite unnecessary affronts to the moral code and the ethical values on which western civilization and society are being built.
In the Swift Current Sun on March 4, 1964, the editor quoted a complaint made to his newspaper about a C.B.C. drama:
Last Tuesday's Quest was the nastiest exhibition of vulgarity that it has been my misfortune to view in all my 80 years of living.
The editor wrote:
Canadian T.V. viewers have got to get it through their heads...that their opinions are not worth a hoot when blown against the C.B.C... . Up to now these C.B.C. arty introverts have been seemingly protected by both the Broadcast Board of Governors and parliament-
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix on March 25, 1964,said:
Every crown corporation is responsible to the government... The majority (of Canadians) oppose censorship. There is a difference between censorship in general and the responsibility of the adult population to the young generation. ... The issue, therefore ... is one of C.B.C. responsibility to sensitive Canadians, young and old...to co-operate... to bring young Canadians into the adult stream of experience, with due cognizance of their years. Instead, the C.B.C. program makers seem to think that they must outrage the nation's sensitivity.

The Deloraine, Manitoba, Times and Star of November 19, 1964, stated editorially:
It ought to be possible to have censorship of good taste which wouldn't really be censorship any more than is the good taste that impels a newspaper editor to see that emphasis is where it belongs.
The Fort William, Ontario Times Journal for October 28, 1964, stated:
Officials of the corporation could probably put up a good argument to back some of the decisions they have made in programming. But that is beside the point. What is needed-and needed badly- is not interference with the work of C.B.C. talent, but a statement of broad policy, agreed to by parliament, by which the organization could work. If such a policy ruled out filth and risque programs, inimical to the wholesome atmosphere of the Canadian home which the C.B.C. was created to serve, much of the present dissatisfaction would disappear.
The Sudbury Star of October 29, 1964 said that "people with high moral values can force television clean-up" and noted that the C.B.C. is "concerned about the extreme and negative reaction" of the promoters of the declaration. The editorial says, "Strong language, perhaps". But it may be the only kind of language that the C.B.C. understands. They do not call for censorship but they do call on members of parliament to make the C.B.C. answerable to the Canadian people. The editorial also noted that the Prime Minister had had complaints from his own riding about "the vulgar filth emitting from some of the programs on C.B.C."
The Owen Sound Sun-Times of October 23, 1964 said:
It must be increasingly evident to C.B.C. management, and to the government, that action must be taken to curb some of the programs which quite evidently menace the basis of society. It would be, of course, much better if that discipline comes from within the crown communication system. But if such is not the case, it is difficult to see how the government can continue to ignore what is quite apparently offensive to a great many Canadians ... it is quite evident that many of those in charge of C.B.C. programming are supporters

Its propaganda should be aimed at the promotion of the good way of life which has marked this nation's history to date, rather than in undermining it.
Then there was an article in the Toronto Star of April 3, 1964 under the heading "In This Corner" by J. B. Lamb. This writer said:
There is a very real need for some measure to be instituted which would bring the viewpoint of Canada's national broadcasting service closer to that of the people it purports to serve and represent. Certainly today the values and ideals which can be attributed to the C.B.C. as a whole, and which are reflected both in the choice of dramatic productions and in comment and panel shows, are not those held by the vast majority of Canadians.
The next is an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of June 10, 1964. Here the editor discusses the remarks of Dr. Wilder Penfield which were made before the Vanier Conference on Family Life at Carle-ton University. The editorial states:
Dr. Penfield dared suggest-and he was applauded -that we should come to some conclusions about the control of mass media so that liberty is not prostituted to licence. Thus a plea for control or even censorship comes not from the old familiar places, but from a man who epitomizes in Canada the most advanced thinking of the scientific mind .. .control...if it is to come in a democratic society... must be imposed by an aroused public insisting that vulgarity shall not be rewarded and degradation shall not be upheld.
Another is the following article on censorship which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of November 7, 1964:
Next to "freedom" and "democracy", the most abased word in the English language, we sometimes think, is "censorship". It used to be that people spoke against sin. . .. What has taken sin's place now, it seems, is "censorship"; let one be tagged ... with wanting to censor something, and the scarlet sins of the vilest sinner become snow white by comparison.. . civilized society exists, and perhaps can only exist, through order, meaning that certain things... are prohibited; censored. Every law ... is a prohibition of something.... Every court .. . every policeman. .. exists to see to it that such laws... be enforced. It is what we mean by "law and order". There is not, never has been and never can be absolute freedom; only freedom in degree.
.. . Thus the right of free speech, as Mr. Justice Holmes put It, is not the right of a man to stand up in a crowded theatre and shout "fire".... No one among us should want censorship without sense, without respect for decent freedoms.... But what

we have a right and need to ask for is censorship, voluntarily or otherwise, of whatever violates accepted codes of public decency, or of public morals, or public security.... In other words ... responsibility. To argue the contrary in the name of "freedom" or in loose thought against "censorship", is to argue against a sense of proportion-to argue in fact for licence and moral anarchy.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on and on with quotations of this type but time does not permit. These quotations are just a sampling of public opinion regarding the C.B.C. as recorded in the English press. Here, then, is the challenge the people of Canada have hurled at them in no uncertain terms. We must not fail the ordinary citizen, the fathers and mothers of this nation who need and want our support in their everyday tasks of family building. The airwaves have been full of the same kind of tragic programming since that time. One could support my argument with almost endless protests that C.B.C. programs which are good and worthy are obliterated by the bad. During these past years we have learned more about the problem. The presence of men and women in positions of program responsibility who openly want to use this great instrument to divide the country and to promote their own peculiar ideologies and personal feelings has been well documented before this house by other speakers from both sides.
I would encourage all members to read carefully the courageous remarks made by the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister in the house last Friday. If you look at the evidence you might wonder whether the hon. member used strong enough words to describe those ruthless few who have been able to get a grip on certain vital programs in the public affairs sector and elsewhere to the great detriment of Canada. The loyalty of some of these men to Canada may indeed be questioned. How devastating have been the policies and actions of some of these men!
We might take the matter of the deliberate promotion of drugs like LSD and marijuana. Over the past two years there have been a series of T.V. and radio programs which have stressed the pleasures of taking LSD for mind expansion and other purposes, supposedly all forward-looking and good. Think of the several exposures of men like Ginsberg who are well known pushers of these drugs and the almost total failure to tell the other side of the story, the tragedy of those hooked by drugs. In the United States, Ginsberg's home country, he has never been able to gain the T.V. exposure he has had in Canada.
November 7. 1967	COMMONS
What do we know about l.s.d.? We are told that it causes a breakdown in chromosomes leading to deformed babies, and almost universally responsible medical opinion warns of the dangers of the misuse of this drug. At least one tragic suicide has taken place in Canada owing to l.s.d. and yet, without adequate research or without giving proper warning, C.B.C. producers have placed before our youngsters programs designed to appeal to youth in which the Ginsbergs and their ilk have told them that this is a good thing. On one French language network program last year, a popular interview show at a prime time, a young reporter told how he took l.s.d. in New York and described its wonders and delights. This same program suggested that it ought to be available without restriction in Canadian grocery and drug stores.
Canadians should stand up in protest against this type of programming. Producers like these should be held accountable in the courts for the death of this Toronto boy and for the wreckage of so many lives. Time does not permit me today to read in detail from some of the editorials which are available. However, I should like to read from an article in the Globe and Mail of November 2, 1967 about one of the favourite subjects of this elite crew of producers and their immediate supervisors-Yorkville and its hippies. The Globe and Mail article by Don Delaplante tells a story that should tear the hearts of parents in this country and certainly ought to make us aware of our responsibility to do the right thing. The article reads in part as follows:
Yesterday, a metro police inspector, members of the College street station plainclothes squad and numerous uniformed officers helped the parents of the girl, a 16-year old Scarboro student turn Yorkville inside out in an effort to find her.... More than 125 girls-
Between the ages of 13 and 20.
-have been arrested so far this year in Yorkville on the charge of vagrancy... . Police are searching Yorkville for 33 girls under 16 whose homes are in metro and for 90 whose homes are out of town... . Police are convinced that a group of older hippies in their late 20's and 30's are preying on the girls as a form of free sex and leading them into prostitution. Police yesterday charged two men aged 25 and 34, with living on the avails of prostitution of Yorkville girls.

The parents of this country will judge whether this is silly or not, Mr. Speaker. The article then continues:

The report of the Aird commission to parliament in 1929, from which our present national system grew, contains certain conclusions relevant and important to Canada today. It recognized several dangers. The first was that broadcasting should be carried out in the interest of Canadian listeners and in the national interest. There is no reference here to the interests of producers. Second, it recognized that where religious broadcasting is allowed there should be regulations prohibiting statements of a controversial nature. It also recognized that broadcasting of political matters should be carefully restricted under arrangements mutually agreed upon by all political parties.
I wish to close with a reference to the frequent attacks on religion which one hears regularly on the C.B.C. and on other programs. This has occurred so often that one can only assume it is a systematic and planned operation. It appears to be some kind of a planned project by a few who seem to work from behind the scenes. This whole aspect of public broadcasting now falls directly on our shoulders. In view of the flagrant misuse of the C.B.C. in the area of religion, I will also be proposing an amendment to protect us against such activities which set Canadians against Canadians, church against church and faith against those of no faith.
I am strongly of the opinion that Canada's national broadcasting system has come under
November 7. 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the influence of a few who are determined to undermine the morals, break down family units and, yes, even the political thinking of Canadians, not through the open forum or normal political activity but rather from inside the T.V. studio. I am also of the opinion that these preconceived opinions of a very small minority, vocal and repetitious as they are, constitute a threat to our liberty.
Others in this house have touched upon certain flagrant failings of our broadcasting system in promoting separatism, division, extreme left-wing politics and extreme leftwing foreign affairs positions. I would endorse all of these accusations against the same smaller group who attack family line. It is from this viewpoint that I speak.
After months and years of discussion by committees and royal commissions the legislation we have before us, while it improves the broadcasting picture immensely, is still without adequate teeth to bring this allimportant aspect of our present modern life under the proper supervision and control of parliament and the people whose tax dollars support it. This is why I have been moved to speak as a parent, to speak on behalf of the families of this nation who are determined and want to raise their children in that kind of life and to be that kind of responsible citizens this nation has had in the past and needs in the future.

Mr. Speaker, in your experience you have heard a multitude of reasons for members participating in debate in this house so I might as well give you mine. My reason is simple. We are discussing Bill C-163 in respect of the C.B.C., but I do not believe we are talking about what the public really wants to know. I hope to be able to explain this statement a little later.
I have listened carefully to the minister's detailed and helpful explanation. Let me congratulate her on her stamina and perseverance. She kept going through all 10,000 words of it. Since then I have listened and read attentively expressions from all corners of this house. I have listened to C.B.C. apologists as well as those who would open up the treasury for five years and those who would curtail expenditures. We have all heard some wonderful legal arguments and opinions that the C.B.C. will now be directed by cabinet. We have heard pious hopes that the ugly spectre of politics will be forever erased from any connection with the C.B.C. There have been other arguments and suggestions that control will now be more political than the 
B.	B.G. ever considered. The more I have heard the more confused the issue has become.
I have formed one opinion with which I am sure the majority of Canadian taxpayers will agree. This debate is missing the target and is skirting the most important consideration in respect of the whole ugly C.B.C. mess. Up to the present time I have discerned no real attempt to come to grips with this important consideration. In the past issues have been clouded by insinuations that any criticism of the C.B.C. is an attempt to direct broadcasting and that parliament must not interfere with the creative elements of the
C.	B.C., with which I agree. There are those who say the C.B.C. is doing a magnificent job. I cannot agree with them. It has been suggested that we should give the C.B.C. enough money to operate for four or five years at a time with no strings attached, but I suggest that the wisdom of this proposal has been challenged by at least four or five programs carried by the C.B.C. network. The Canadian taxpayer would like parliament to make sure that the C.B.C. is financially responsible. I do not believe for one moment that the people are as overly concerned about programming as we have been led to believe. They still have control of the on and off button. What they want parliament to find out is the value we are receiving from this expenditure.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat spoke about the terrible programming on the C.B.C. With all respect I suggest to him that no one has to watch any program. They can shut it off. I have heard public indignation about the expenditure of in excess of $100 million per year on this giant. This is understandable when one considers the other segments of our society which are suffering for lack of money. For example, what might an extra $100 million have done in respect of housing in Canada this year?
Let me say again that this debate is missing the target by a country mile with few exceptions. Last night the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) got close to the point, but I fear he is not prepared to vote the way he talks.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
You see, Mr. Speaker, we are taking off in all directions simultaneously even though the basic issue must be: How can we control and, yes, cut down on the woeful extravagances of this juggernaut? I submit, respectfully, that nothing in the bill and not much said in the
November 7, 1967

debate so far has shown the way to reduce
costs or to really improve programming- nothing.
As things stand now, the minister accepts no responsibility. The stock answer is always that she is not responsible, that she only reports for the C.B.C. Most of us have had experience with the complaint of a constituent about C.B.C. service-and what a laugh this is. What these constituents have received in the mail from a highly paid public relations expert is a snow job beyond compare, so that the poor constituent really does not know what his question was in the first place. I understand that all this is to be changed, but I get the inference from the debate that the final answer to most disputes will now rest with cabinet.
Most politicians, indeed all politicians, need a certain amount of publicity, so I suggest that a politician who dares to criticize the C.B.C. is certainly leaving himself or herself subject to blacklisting. It seems to me that the bigger the apologist for the C.B.C., the more coverage he may receive. It is, therefore, indeed a brave front bench member of parliament who has the temerity to say anything critical of this monopolistic creature. Some have tried in the past but they have been immediately charged with trying to control programming and other sinister behaviour. It has been said that no one should criticize this sacred cow. But now the minister has and she has been criticized for her actions. I do not agree too often with the minister on other things but in this regard I have to give her full marks.
Hear, hear.
The only criticism I have to offer is that she should have done it years ago and then have been backed up by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
Hear, hear.

I am only a lowly backbencher who gets little publicity in any event, but I suggest that the C.B.C. has gotten so far out of hand that the only cure for this financial cancer is to offer it for sale or lease to private interests. Buyers can be found. I am all the more convinced that this is the only "out" since there is absolutely no consensus in the house.
Even the bill does not conform to the unanimous report of the committee on broadcasting. I believe there has been such a build-up of power cells, so much feather-beddding. so many working to rule arrange-

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting ments and other inefficient practices built up over the years that nothing as mild as the minister's suggested shake-up in management can really break this hold on the organization. Truly it is bureaucracy run rampant. As a matter of fact, I would not object to a temporary shutdown, perhaps a few lay-offs or terminations. It might be necessary to cease programming operations for a few days or weeks, but this would be a cheap price to pay if we could get this financial cancer removed from the public's back.
When the Broadcasting Act was first enacted some 30 years ago Canada had just emerged from the horse and buggy days. We then used the Morse code for communication and the telegraph operator was quite a big man. Places were not hours apart, as is the case today, but days and days apart. The high principle of tying the country together and unifying it was different then from what it is now. I suggest this was well put by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Ballard) when he said that the concept then was entirely different from what it is today.
I still subscribe to this worth-while aim and would be prepared to have the C.B.C. subsidized, and in turn to have the C.B.C. subsidize capital equipment expenditures to provide service, that is, a signal, to every' Canadian. As the minister said, the rule of thumb is that a community of 2,000 should have television and a community of 500 should have radio. But for heavens sake let us get out of programming and management by remote control. Let us stop subsidizing mediocrity. Let us make the producing and programming part of this organization selfsupporting.
I can hear it now. It will be said we are stifling talent or doing this or that. But I submit that talent, both performing and creative, that is worth while will survive. True talent always has. But let us stop this silly habit of substituting berets and beards for talent. Let us substitute real talent for this ersatz variety. The only way this can be done is to make them cut the mustard and go to work.
Let us take a simple example. We do not have too many Barbra Striesands or Lena Hornes in Canada but we do have some very talented people. Let us compare the operation of a North American commercial network presenting talent. The presentation will be on a plain, attractive stage with adequate lighting, but with talent. I repeat, talent. The C.B.C. will probably reproduce the Taj

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting enterprise should be accepted. It must work in unison with public enterprise; one part private, one part public. I would like to see how it is done.
Give the C.B.C. a little private enterprise, and you will see that things will change. In my opinion, we could run the C.B.C. with $100 million and save $45 million by bringing in responsible people, employees who are satisfied with their salaries, their expenses, and who work from nine or ten o'clock in the morning until four or four thirty in the afternoon, taking coffee breaks, as we say even in French, in the morning and in the afternoon.
In saying this, Mr. Speaker, I do not mean that employees should be treated like slaves. No.
Des pauses-cafe.

Yes, it is "pause-cafe" in French. I thank my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi, who is perfectly bilingual. But note that he did not say "pousse-cafe", but "pause-cafe", which is quite different.
Mr. Speaker, we must surely take corrective measures with regard to the C.B.C. management. Who will be the next president? We do not know. Only, let him be able to assume his responsibilities and be responsible, otherwise, as I said earlier, let us get rid of the C.B.C. and sell it to private enterprise. First, it would put an end to our present discussions and allow us perhaps to watch better shows or programs than those now being produced.
Mind you, this does not mean that we are granting full freedom to say or do everything on radio and television. We can always resort to the B.B.G. to present immoral radio or television programs from being shown. There is also legislation which parliament can pass. We can establish in Canada a broadcasting authority which would ensure that the shows and programs presented are such as to serve the best interests of our population and enrich the minds of our compatriots.
This is possible, because as things are going now, Mr. Speaker, next year, when we again consider the estimates of the C.B.C., they will not be around $145 million but they will be increased again. We might be up to $160 or $170 million by then, whereas private enterprise, I repeat, operates at about 50 or 60 per cent cheaper than the crown corporation. Counting on the fact that it is a crown corporation, that the people pay and the government votes the estimates they say: "Let's
3992	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting go". Money is spent haphazardly; it does not matter, as long as it is spent. As I said a while ago, there are loafers in the C.B.C. I, myself, have seen these well-paid loafers. Loafers, that means lazy people and there are enough of them; so let us eliminate them. Just for the sake of keeping somebody's job, are we going to keep on spending public moneys as we are doing now?
I know my words will irritate Mr. Ouimet and many others. But what I say is true, and we have all had proof of that. What I am saying now really happens, I am not making it up. When I say that separatists have been treated with kid gloves by the C.B.C. in the province of Quebec, I speak the truth. I gave as an example earlier the case of Aylmer, last night. In the case of Montreal, the fights in P;errefonds, for example, how did the C.B.C. happen to be there? Because there are separatists working for the C.B.C.
Mr. Speaker, it is time for us to take a stand. Somebody has already said that the province of Quebec is just as smart as the others, and I really do believe that. However, there as elsewhere, there are people who only see one side of the coin and who cannot get along with the other people.
I heard Mr. Rene Levesque say in Vancouver the other day that there is no French problem there. Then he says: It is true and Premier Bennett is right; so French Canadians, come and live in the province of Quebec.
Which premier?

Mr. Bennett: Go and live in the province of Quebec. Fine solution. We have more unemployed in Quebec than anywhere else in Canada. Let us add them to our own jobless.
Mr. Speaker, for six years, I have been asking the Conservative government when it was in office, and the Liberal government, to give our French-speaking population in western Canada, the service of our national radio and television network, and it has not been done yet. I was told, the other day, that the radio coverage would be extended to Vancouver-Victoria, as of November 1.
The 4th of December.

Well, now it will start on December 4; that is a month and four days later than I was told. I am happy to hear that the radio service will start on December 4 and the western French-Canadian minority will be delighted to get it. However, they also
EMr. Caouette.]
DEBATES	November 7, 1967
want television service. When $145 million are available, instead of sending a large portion of it to Viet Nam, the Congo and Africa, we should begin by extending coverage to western Canada, to people who are Canadians the same as we are. They can get the English network. When an English network was requested for Malartic, in Abitibi, in my riding, I exerted pressures so that our English-speaking citizens could get that television station, served by Timmins. Today they have it.
Some will reply that it is not as far between Timmins and Malartic as it is in the west and I agree, but if we had started extending the service towards Vancouver six years ago, do you not think that it would have reached Vancouver by now?
But no, they prefer to go to Viet Nam. Is Viet Nam closer to us than Vancouver? Is the Congo closer to us? Is Africa closer to us? Is Moscow closer to us?
When I went to Moscow two years ago there were C.B.C. people there. I met some in London who found it hard to take the trouble of meeting us when we arrived.
It is the same thing in Paris.
We arrived at 7 or 7.15 in the morning and there was not a soul from the C.B.C. to greet us.
It was too early.

It was a delegation from the Canadian parliament which was going on a special mission to Moscow. There was not a single representative from the C.B.C.; no, that is for the others. They are well paid by us, though. If we were to refuse them the money to pay their salary, they would go on strike.
In Paris, it is the same thing. I will not give any names, but I could name one I called up on the telephone at two o'clock in the morning, in London, to ask him: ''What are you doing? Are you not coming to meet us?" His answer was. "Oh, you know, I was not too well aware of your arrival". He was not aware. If a coloured man from Africa had arrived there, he would have been immediately aware of it. He was not aware of it at the C.B.C.
Hear, hear.

But they knew about Aylmer.
November 7, 1967

Oh, yes, they were in Aylmer. When we went to Iran last year, the same thing happened. They do not see us, but we receive reports from all the corners of the world; they are there and paid by us. When parliamentary representatives travel in those countries, they are unseen, they can no longer be seen.
Mr. Speaker, it is time to make a complete sweep with a vacuum cleaner and remove that rottenness, because it reminds me of the Augean stables where 3,000 head of cattle had not been cleaned for 30 years. Hercules had to divert a river to clean those stables.
I think that it would be high time to divert the St. Lawrence river to clean the stables of the C.B.C. An hon. member just said that the St. Lawrence is polluted. Let us use the Ottawa river.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take any more of the time of the house; on the other hand, I do want to say I support wholeheartedly what the Secretary of State has said about certain sectors of the C.B.C.
It is high time we prescribe the necessary remedial action. Now, Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-163 allows the members to make suggestions, but not to sling mud, as Mr. Ouimet says, and to give recognition to those who in the C.B.C. are competent and perform their duties with dignity. There are some, they are in a majority. But the C.B.C. officials should take their responsibilities and give the Canadian people programs of value, programs worthy of the C.B.C., in short programs which will be the pride of the Canadian nation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that next to the defence of the realm this is the most important subject to come up this year, namely, whether we are going to socialize the airwaves and, if we try, can we make it work. I read in tonight's Ottawa Journal the headline "Judy Stands Alone In C.B.C. Uproar." I want to tell you right now, Mr. Speaker, that she does not.
Hear, hear.

She represents a great cross-section of the Canadian people and their thinking on this matter. This is too big a subject to be buried in partisan politics. In this situation the hon. lady has to speak out. She is not only a minister of the crown but she has a responsibility to parliament and the Canadian people to be the champion of the

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting freedom of the airwaves, which I claim is today very seriously threatened.
I should like to think that a mere change of management in the C.B.C. would settle these problems once and for all. Perhaps we could get a Donald Gordon or a Mr. Fisher to take over the job of policing the C.B.C.
Which Fisher?

But will this by itself correct the situation? It will not unless we stand behind the hon. lady, who has the responsibility of reporting to parliament on the C.B.C., when she uses forthright, if a little colourful, language. Unfortunately, from the beginning we tried to put the C.B.C. beyond the control of parliament and make it a crown corporation which would be above parliament. The result has been disastrous.
If we could And such a person to head the C.B.C.-I understand we are having some difficulty and are not exactly swamped with offers for this very important job-would he be backed up? Presumably the only way he could be backed up when he got into a pitched battle with the directors would be by appealing to the hon. lady or her successor. How much backing can he expect? I suspect that it is not fear which keeps the hon. lady from naming the people. She could name them; in fact, we all know who they are. If she does not want to name them, I am certainly not afraid to do so. I will read the list; they are well known to us all: Patrick Watson, Laurier LaPierre, Pierre Berton, Douglas Leiterman, Reeves Haggan, Sidney Bronstein, and such fringe benefit boys as Mr. Chaput and Mr. Levesque who are assisting in the plot to reduce Canada to a motley collection of fractured institutions.
Anybody who has been around for the last three years, has had his ears open and has watched a television set knows perfectly well that there is an unmistakable pattern connected with the difficulties experienced throughout the C.B.C. We are getting propaganda by concentration on only the negative side of questions. We do not hear the positive side.
Let us consider our young people. The young people of today are depicted on the C.B.C. over and over again as nothing but hippies. They all want the pill, they all want abortions, they all want free love. No such nonsense was ever before presented to the Canadian people. A good 90 per cent of the Canadian people, young people particularly, are just as fine as we or our parents were.

Hear, hear.
November 7, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting

But they are not being heard. It is not true that most of our young people are hippies and think in this vein. Only about 10 per cent of our young people fall into this category. That 10 per cent will always be with us. They are incapable of making rational decisions in their lives. It is terribly dangerous to bastardize the Canadian airwaves by encouraging only the negative, only the filthy, only the ugly.
Our young people have a right and a heritage, and I am glad the hon. lady has taken the step to at least bring this matter out into the open where something can and will be done about it. Nobody heading the C.B.C. today can say he does not know where the problem lies. I do not think anybody would take on this job unless he was a man of great courage, because it will not be an easy task. He may have to fight alone. If parliament will not get together and provide a little more solid backing for the people who know where the trouble is and are willing to take steps to correct it, I do not think we can expect to find anybody to take on the job.
This is a dual problem involving both management and programming. If anybody thinks there is any doubt whatever that this is right, I should like to spend a moment or two reading into the record evidence to support my contention. In a recent survey of C.B.C. programming it was shown that 80 items touched on American subjects or on the United States itself. Sixty-two out of the 80 were either overtly anti-American or played on United States problems and ills. Sixteen items dealt with the Viet Nam war. Fifteen out of the 16 items created impressions opposed to the United States role in Viet Nam and could have brought nothing but comfort and encouragement to Hanoi.
There have been complaints by Canadian diplomatic officials abroad who have been dismayed at the variance between what has been observed by them on the spot abroad and the impressions created by the C.B.C. With respect to communism, on 14 programs communism was given sympathetic treatment. Not once in the last two years was there any substantial criticism of a communist country or a communist philosophy. The Patrick Watson-Roy Faibish film, "The 700 Million", praising the accomplishments of mainland China and produced after 62 days in that country, was broadcast on no less than three occasions across this nation.


[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It showed nothing but happy, cheerful people, which, to me at least appears to be in strange contrast to the stories now coming through of the terrorist activities of the Red Guard. Young China now has no god but Mao.
The C.B.C. has not left religion alone. I do not say that we should only see people worshipping on Picture Page but it is passing strange that apparently there is nothing good and worthy of note going on any more in the Christian world. On 28 occasions Seven Days dealt with religious subjects and 22 of these programs were sarcastic or antagonistic in presenting some bizarre and unrepresentative aspect of religion. In the last program the slogan "Kill a Commie for Christ" was repeated several times. The United Church Observer, which by the way has become very broadminded, commented as follows on June 1:
When they did an item on religion, as they frequently did, it was likely to be a distortion of the bizarre.
That is an understatement if I ever heard one.
All the 29 programs produced by the C.B.C. concerning racial problems played up bitterness, injustice or extremism. Nothing was produced to show the notable advances made in legislation, education or in other areas. As everyone knows, this is not an easy subject to handle, but why is the negative side always shown? I say there is a plot, a well thought out and clever plot to reduce Canada to a group of fractured institutions.
I wish wholeheartedly that I could vote for the bill because it contains points with which I certainly agree. It says that the C.B.C. should promote national unity. I took careful count of all the programs I saw relating to national unity during the last year and I noted that some 70 per cent were on the negative side. There was limitless coverage of men such as Levesque and Chaput. One would think they are the only men of some standing. What opportunity is there for men like myself to say: I believe in a united Canada, a Canada of equal opportunity, a Canada without compulsion and without prejudice? I would like to see all members of this house get up and give their views on the subject. I venture to say that the Chaputs and the Levesques would be outnumbered by a hundred to one.
The minister finds herself in a bind. How can she be loyal to her party and to the
November 7, 1967	COMMONS
cabinet and still tell us the truth? The whole structure of the C.B.C. is soft at the top and rotten at the bottom.
I thought it was the other way around.

In less happy days I had to make my living as a lumberman and when there was a rotten tree in the bush the old, wise lumbermen said, "Do not shake the rotten tree". They called it "widow-maker". They said, "The top will come down and crush you". And so it would. I am sorry to see that we have had to wait for a lady to dare to shake the tree. Perhaps she is not afraid of being a widow. But I hope the whole rotten tree falls on someone and falls on him fast.
I would like to support what my colleague the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon) said, namely, that we should send the subject matter of the bill to the committee. Will the committee unearth any more truth than we have already? We know the problem. The only thing that faces us is the solution to that problem, but if we pass the bill-and I have no doubt it will be passed because I believe it is a sincere effort to get to the root of the matter-will we give it the backing it deserves? Will we live up to it and decide to keep the airwaves of Canada free, clean and fit for the fine people who are still around, who have not been brainwashed and who still believe that their church, their school and their government will give of their best, people who have not all lost their nerve and have not subjected themselves to the defeatism which is only too rampant?
If there is no one in Canada who can handle the job of leading the C.B.C., then we had better appoint a board to do it. Perhaps we should give it a try because time is running out. Perhaps this bill will provide us with an answer. I am not prepared to say it will, but I think it is high time we stopped allowing this Tower of Babel called the C.B.C. to keep us disunited. I would hate to have to tear it down because I believe there is a future for the C.B.C. if we can solve the problems with which it has faced us. We need a great "E" for education, a great "E" for entertainment and a great "E" for excellence. If there are no people in this country who know the difference between filth and excellence perhaps we will have to import somebody who does, because I do not see the filth and degradation being peddled over the airwaves in the United States, which is so maligned by some of my friends, that I see in

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the northern half of this continent which I always hoped and believed would give some leadership in this field.
I am a politician and I suppose I am unfit to undertake a job of this kind. It is not from lack of nerve or lack of knowledge of the subject because I know a rotten tree when I see one and I know that the sooner we cut it down and plant another clean, decent, strong one in its place, the better. When we get it there, let us have a fire guard and let us have someone with the know-how and the power to ensure that all our trees survive because we still need their shade and the fresh air which can only come from a living, clean-limbed tree.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
En anglais, s'il vous plait.

Yes, sir. I heard the hon. member mention the names of two men as prospects for the job which Mr. Ouimet will be vacating shortly. He mentioned a certain Mr. Fisher. I know of two men by that name who are well known nationally. Would the hon. gentleman please tell us which one he meant?

I should like to clear up the misapprehension I may have created. I did not suggest either of these men as an ideal head of the C.B.C. I pointed out one facet of their character, namely courage. Mr. John Fisher has courage. He is a great salesman for Canada. Similarly, I have no doubt whatsoever about the other Mr. Fisher. If he wants to use his talents in this capacity, I believe he is quite capable and he has the courage to do so. Mr. Donald Gordon has made a great contribution to Canadian life and I am quite sure he has the courage to look into the mess, clean out the garbage and replace it with something of some merit.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. Before the hon. member for Verdun makes such a statement about what I said I would appreciate it very much if he would read the text of my remarks tomorrow. If he does, I do not think he will make the statement he has made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I do not need to read the text. I take the hon. gentleman at his word and I apologize if I misconstrued what he said. I was under the impression that he suggested the time had come to abolish the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If he did not, I apologize. For that matter, this suggestion was advanced by a fellow member of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman), last night in a very entertaining speech, one which I enjoyed but with which I did not necessarily agree.
I think it is significant that Canadians in general depreciate anything that is Canadian and can see no good in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. With one eye on the clock, perhaps I could take the seven minutes available to me to point out the rather paradoxical attitude of most of the members of the official opposition when they castigate the C.B.C., praise the minister for her recent declaration and then engage in what I regard as rather unwarranted attacks on the hon. lady during the question period. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Bigg), who I thought spoke well and sincerely. He was not critical of the present Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), and I was rather pleased about that because it seems to me the hon. lady has been subjected to rather harsh treatment during the question period.
I have wondered about the furore in the house, particularly during the question period, over the fact that the Secretary of State simply said, in her own colourful style, what

many boards that have been set up to investigate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have said over the last decade. I believe the Fowler report mentioned at least 11 points which were found to conform with the findings of the internal committee set up by the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At the same time, I do not believe it is particularly appropriate that we should spend our time in castigating Mr. Ouimet, as some members have been doing. I think it has been very obvious to all of us who have been concerned with the problems of broadcasting, and I sat for some time on that particular committee, that there is a great malaise in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I suppose the internal set-up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be modified, but that is what this bill is all about.
I do not believe that in today's world it is necessary that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be considered a competitor of private broadcasting. The corporation should, rather, be considered as an alternative for Canadians. I believe that we are too prone to forget the degree of assimilation of things that are Canadian by our good friends, the United States. If we are to survive as a nation we have to retain control over our communication media. I know of no better way of maintaining control over the media of communication in this country than by having a strong, viable Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which will fulfil its role. I think we agree that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not been able to achieve its potential in television. It has been seeking for leadership and until very recently that leadership has not been forthcoming. I believe this is something that is evident in the Glassco report, the Fowler report, the president's committee report, the white paper, and we found this to be so in the broadcasting committee.
At the same time, I must say I was quite impressed with Mr. Ouimet as an individual when he appeared before the committee. He was extremely loyal to the organization over which he presided. He may have been a little reluctant in some areas or in agreeing with the general assessment of members, but I found him to be a very good advocate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, very knowledgeable and very forthright in his answers. I do not believe Mr. Ouimet should be singled out as the sole cause of the problems that confront the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation now. When I listened to
November 7, 1967

some of the speeches made during this debate I wondered if they had not been written by a Barry Goldwater or a Ronald Reagan. It seemed to me that the solution to the problem suggested by one hon. member was that Canadians should never see anything except "Anne of Green Gables". I do not believe we are going to do a job for the Canadian people by protecting them from exposure to provocative programs. I know that in the opinion of many, including myself, there is a very thin line between a provocative program and outright smut and filth.
Certainly, as one who participated in all the deliberations of the committee on the Seven Days question, I feel that where the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Mr. Ouimet were amiss was in not firing some of the people responsible for lack of judgment. The same people were responsible for the bias in that program which was obvious from the day it was conceived. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, June 29, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-105, to incorporate Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation-Mr. Orange-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

subtopic: RAINBOW PIPE LINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two with regard
Private Bills
to this bill before it passes. It presents the house with a very interesting problem. From time to time we hear a good deal of talk about ownership of Canadian industry by Canadians, and we hear a great deal of talk urging Canadians to take a greater part in controlling Canada's destiny. This bill, Mr. Chairman, in my opinion provides a prime example of the area in which Canadians should move.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The former minister of finance has written many books, most of them saying that Canadians should control their own industrial development and that it should not be controlled by foreigners. This private bill shows the area of endeavour where Canadians ought to exert themselves. Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation wishes to build a pipe line into the Northwest Territories. In committee we asked whether in granting permission to build such a pipe line we would be granting a monopoly right to transport oil, gas or solids in the years ahead from the Northwest Territories to the rest of Canada. The reply was that a second pipe line could be built, of course, but it is obvious that a second pipe line would be uneconomical and probably would not be built. If permission to build this pipe line is granted the company to be incorporated will be given monopoly rights.
The company was also asked whether it would allow Canadians to subscribe to its shares. One of those answering for the company said, "Well, first we want to be incorporated, we must appear before the Energy Board, but at this time we really have no intention of allowing Canadians to participate." I want to know how this attitude is to be taken in the light of exhortations to Canadians to take a greater interest in their industrial development and to exercise greater control over their industries and resources. Are we to give this company seeking incorporation a monopoly in the Northwest Territories where, as far back as the early 1920's, oil was discovered? Are we to give this company, which does not want Canadians to participate in it, a monopoly?
Who will control this company? It is said that Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation is to be controlled partly by Imperial Oil Limited, which is a company controlled in the United States, partly by Mobil Oil of Canada Limited, another company controlled in the United States, and partly by the Acquitaine group which in essence is a corporation controlled by the French government. Are three foreign

November 7, 1967'
Private Bills
concerns to be allowed to come before this house during private members' hour and ask for a monopoly to move oil from one part of Canada to another?
This matter strikes at the very heart of my Canadianism. I want to participate or at least I want the privilege or being allowed to do so should I wish to. I am interested in Canada, as others are. Look at the interest Canadians showed in the Athabasca tar sands. That venture was oversubscribed by Canadians. Something like $12 million was permitted to be subscribed by Canadians and many were turned away after the venture was oversubscribed. Albertans were turned away. They were also turned away after many Canadians had oversubscribed the Alberta gas trunk line which was developed in Alberta some years ago.
Why are Canadians not to be allowed to participate in this entity which seeks incorporation? Some personnel of the company have said, "Oh, well, this is a speculative venture and therefore Canadians will not want to participate in it." Canadians should say for themselves whether they wish to participate. At least they should have the opportunity of participating and the opportunity of eventually controlling the company.
What is to happen here? Eventually control of the entity seeking incorporation may vest in the Aquitaine group which is controlled by the French government. That is not a healthy picture and is not one that should commend itself to those who took the former minister of finance seriously.
It is all very well for some to say that Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation is to build a line to the Zama field which is inside the Northwest Territories and that Canadian companies may, should they wish, hook another pipe line into that of Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation. That argument is beside the point. Once the pipe line is built the company seeking incorporation will be the major mover of oil and commodities in the area and, as I have said, it will be uneconomical to build another pipe line. Because the company moves something like 8 per cent of the oil produced in Alberta it should not be given a monopoly for the entire Northwest Territories, which has enormous proven oil reserves.
In the 1920's the Norman Wells oil field was discovered to contain reserves. Is this house to allow this company a monopoly to operate in that area? I hope that other hon. members will vigorously oppose passage of

this bill. Until provision is made for Canadians to subscribe to the capital stock of the company and for Canadians to control it eventually, we should resist its passage. We in Canada have the right to guide our own destiny in the years ahead.

subtopic: RAINBOW PIPE LINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to say anything today. Nevertheless I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Acadia on what he has said and say that I could not agree with him more.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The history of the discovery of the Rainbow oil field is the best argument I know for the creation of a Canada development corporation or a resources development corporation-call it what you will. What happened originally is a national disgrace. At the time of the original discovery Mr. Rudolph, president of Banff Oil, tried to find capital in Canada. He was not able to do so and as a result this viable oil field fell into the hands of a United States company and the Aquitaine group controlled by the French government. Had we at that time been able to rely upon the services of a resource development corporation I am confident that at the very least we could have maintained majority ownership in Canadian hands.
A development corporation need not enter into the actual development of oil fields or oil pools as a majority partner, but there is no reason why it would not become involved as a minority partner once an oil field or oil bed has been discovered. Indeed, its objectives might go beyond that. The corporation might also be concerned with search, exploration and development work in areas of the north where oil bodies have not yet been discovered.
There is no reason why the activities of such a corporation should cause fear or apprehension in business circles. There is no reason, in my opinion, why private mining interests in Canada should hesitate to accept the existence of a government minority role in endeavours of this sort.
The federal government has full jurisdiction over the natural resources of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. There is no constitutional controversy about that. Today the Supreme Court confirmed the jurisdiction of the federal government over offshore mineral rights. So there is no reason why the federal government through a resource development corporation should not participate,

hand in hand with private interests, in the [DOT]exploration and development of these resources. Surely direct participation by the *Canadian people through its government would be a unifying factor in this country's development. Of course, it is only in the areas I have mentioned, where the federal government has complete jurisdiction over national resources, that we would be completely free from charges of interference with provincial rights. The arguments in favour of the establishment of a development corporation are so overwhelming as to make me hopeful that the government will not delay further in setting up such a corporation.
All this has a bearing upon the particular matter which is before the house at the moment, the establishment of a company to build a pipe line from the Northwest Territories into western Canada. I wish that the wise head of the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie rested on the shoulders of some cabinet members so that they could see the wisdom of the remarks he has made and the remarks that we of the C.C.F. and N.D.P. have been making for many years. The suggestion that the bill not be proceeded with until guarantees of this sort are given is a commendable one.
Like the hon. member for Acadia I too am quite concerned about the degree to which not only this proposed company but many other companies which are controlled by people who do not even live in Canada own our natural resources without that sort of responsibility to Canada which Canadians would have. The N.D.P. has been in the forefront of this fight for a long time now. Hon. members know that on every occasion upon which a bill to incorporate some kind of company with the element of foreign ownership in it

The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development thought that this practice should no longer continue. He did not think it was good enough for the people in the

Northwest Territories that industry should come in, develop and exploit the raw materials of the natural resource, and then leave as quickly as they can, taking with them the profits, after they have moved the raw material out of the territories to some other part of the nation or to some other part of the world in order that it can be developed, manufactured and refined.

The consequences of this are very bad indeed because it means in effect that the people who live in the area obtain just the bare minimum amount of income and employment form the natural resources in the area. It means also that Canada as a whole suffers, because in order for us to become a nation, with some force to our economy, a nation in which we can establish a continually rising standard of living, we must put more effort into transforming our natural resources into the finished products at points as close as possible to the sites of the raw materials, and in particular in the nation itself.
