I find myself in complete agreement with the hon. member for Acadia who touched upon the two main points in issue here. There is one additional point I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. It is wise that we understand that the three companies involved, namely Imperial Oil, Mobiloil and Banff-Aquitaine, will each own 33J per cent of the stock. I should point out that Banff will own 3-J per cent and the Aquitaine group will own 30 per cent, so together they will own 33 J per cent.
It is fair to say that two of these companies have no financial base in Canada in the sense that Canadians own stock in these companies, and I refer to Mobiloil and Banff-Aquitaine. This emphasizes the point made by the hon. member for Acadia. Since there is no opportunity for Canadians to purchase the stock of these companies, there is no way in which Canadians could in the long run purchase these companies, something which I would hope could happen in respect of most companies of this type in Canada in the long run.
Surely it is completely wrong for us to give a new company special privileges such as those sought through this bill. Some of us

have had conversations with the president of Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation which would indicate that in the near future an opportunity will be provided Canadians to purchase stock of this company. I have been informed today that this company has put $10 million worth of first mortgage bonds on the market. At first glance one might think the company has gone some way in correcting the disadvantage we see in respect of foreign owned companies operating in Canada. However, if one looks at this situation he must agree that this is not so. What the company is in fact asking us to do is contribute our money to the company's development, with the company retaining complete control. The ownership of bonds does not give the owner the right to vote or an opportunity to share in the profits. One does get his money back, with interest, but does not share in the profits of any large development the company may undertake in the future.
There is one other point which should be made in respect of this company. There is a provision which would allow the company to use its funds, or the funds of the Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation-and we should be careful to make that distinction-for exploring and developing wells any place in the Northwest Territories. This means the corporation need not show any profit and will be able to avoid paying income or corporation taxes in this way. The company could readily use its profit from the pipe line operation for exploration and development. We have been assured that this is not the intention. Perhaps we should accept that statement, but the opportunity is there. Consequently I feel that this provision requires some modification before the bill is passed.
In my opinion this is a bad bill and I cannot support it.

specifically to the testimony of Mr. Bredin. When dealing with the tax advantage aspect of this proposition he said quite clearly and unequivocally that one of the purposes for establishing this pipe line corporation was to allow it to enter into a field of activity quite apart from its prime purpose, the transmission of petroleum. We have not been told the extent to which it might get into this activity of the oil and gas business in order to take advantage of certain sections of the Income Tax Act. It is not clear to me why a subsidiary of parent firms which are already in the gas and oil production business would want to take part in the same business. We have been told that there would be tax advantages and that the company could apply under our income tax laws for certain write-offs or deduction of expenses for drilling and developping.
It is true under existing law that a pipe line corporation must act as a common carrier, but it is difficult to find out accurately the extent to which this fact will have any practical result. This company if incorporated by this parliament would have to act as a common carrier. But in fact whose products would it be carrying? It seems to me that in the immediate period after incorporation, if incorporation were granted, it would be carrying only the products of the firms that are parent to it, and no corporations engaged in the oil and gas business in this part of the country would be able to avail themselves of the service this common carrier would have to provide.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting developed to a sufficient quantity. I say to the committee that there is no real urgency to pass this bill today. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the supper hour I had an opportunity to speak for six or seven minutes on the bill before us. At that time I pointed out that I found it rather paradoxical that the same people who paid tribute to the Secretary of State for her recent statements pertaining to the C.B.C. and who said it was a true reflection of the feeling of most Canadians and of most members of the house would take advantage of the question period to castigate her, to suggest her resignation and to attempt to embarrass her. It is ironic that the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) who appeared to be very concerned with the minister's statement went even farther when we were discussing the very controversial program "This Hour Has Seven Days" in the broadcasting committee.
I think the minister has probably done us all a favour in stating concisely in her own colourful terms what essentially had been said on numerous occasions by the investigating bodies that had been set up over almost a decade to examine the operations of the C.B.C. I also stated that I felt this was not the time to criticize the president of the C.B.C., as some hon. members have done. I think that he has served this country well and has done his best as president of the corporation. He has presided over the C.B.C.'s operations at a time when the corporation has found it difficult indeed to make the transformation from radio to television. My personal view, as one who has sat on that particular committee, is that the whole structure of the C.B.C. management has become too unwieldy and, as has been pointed out in many briefs, editorials and articles, communication between management and what we like to call the creative force has been limited. I think this was best exemplified by the debate on the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" when it became obvious to us
November 7, 1967

that the producers of this particular program had little or no supervision for almost two years. This resulted in the unfortunate incidents which marred that television season.
I know the minister would like to get the bill through this evening and I know there are one or two other speakers who would like to participate at this stage of the debate. At present there is an amendment before us which must be disposed of. If the amendment is accepted it will not result in a defeat of the government or the minister, but will rather be a defeat for all members of parliament in that perhaps we will not have done justice to the very progressive bill which is before us for second reading. The issue that is before the house is the acceptance or rejection of the principle of the bill, which is the formation of a new board or a new medium to control not only the C.B.C. but also private industry and, what is more important, the implementation of a national broadcasting policy.
I was very impressed by the minister's speech last week. I thought it covered all the points and left the door open for desirable amendments when the bill reaches the committee stage. The minister made it quite obvious to everyone that she would welcome constructive criticism and any amendments that may be proposed at the committee stage which would improve the bill, and this is the function of parliament. Clearly that function would be circumvented were we to accept the amendment before the house, which would kill the bill and, what is more, kill the principle, to which we all adhere, that Canada needs a national broadcasting policy.
As is always the case when we discuss a subject as emotional as the C.B.C., extreme suggestions are made from many parts of the house, as was the case today when several members proposed that the C.B.C. be eliminated. I do not happen to share that view and I am entitled to my opinion as are other people. I do not happen to think that private broadcasting has done such a wonderful job in the country. There is really no relationship between the programming on private radio and television stations, when we compare their day to day operations, and the promises they usually make when they are seeking a licence. I have no television station in my own riding, although I have one of the finest radio stations in North America. I say this as a result of the many awards which CKVL has won in international competition. I come from an area of the country in which we do 27053-2531
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting have a choice of many programs on television since we have the dubious privilege of watching United States television stations which are beamed into our homes directly across the border.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
If we, as Canadians, are to discover the greatness of this country and reach the potential promised in this centennial year, then it is imperative that we should have control over the medium of communications. We have taken steps in previous years to maintain some degree of control over newspapers. I feel it is equally important that we maintain control over all mediums of communication. If management has not been up to par, has not given the leadership necessary, then this is no reflection on the corporation itself. This is a reflection upon management, and perhaps upon government for allowing these positions to remain open for such a length of time. There is nothing wrong with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation per se. It exists and must continue to exist.
I believe that the standard set by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is one which private broadcasting tries to equal or surpass and is a constant reminder that there are alternatives to private radio and private television. I often wonder what the standards of private radio and television would be if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were not available as an alternative or to provide competition. We have the same situation in connection with the railways, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, in connection with the airways and in connection with many other fields of our economic life.
There are I think some very laudable objectives in this bill. For instance there is the statement in one section of the bill that Canadians are entitled to broadcasting services in English and in French as public funds become available. This is an objective that private radio and television would not meet. Private broadcasting would not meet that objective because it would not necessarily be profitable. There was a void in the Toronto area in French language broadcasting, and private enterprise did not move into1 that area. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has done so and will continue to do so-in many other parts of the country where, because of population or geographical reasons it is not feasible for private industry to operate a station at a profit, as they are entitled to do.
November 7, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Now, Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot said about separatism, particularly within Radio Canada. This brings me to another objective of the bill, and that is that the broadcasting systems in Canada should work for the cause of national unity. There is a connection between this desirable objective of broadcasting and the separatist movement in the province of Quebec, and the degree to which the separatists have or have not infiltrated the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I suspect there are many separatists working for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There are separatists in the House of Commons. There are separatists working in the railways and in all fields of endeavour. I feel it is safe to say that in the province of Quebec about 10 per cent of the population endorses separatism for one reason or another. By the law of averages, some of these people of course have to be working for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. However, whatever we do about separatists in the corporation, Mr. Speaker, we cannot do as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) suggests and show "Anne of Green Gables" five hours a night. As I said earlier, when I listened to his speech I was not sure whether he wrote it or whether Barry Goldwater or Ronald Reagan wrote it. It reflects reactionary policy, which I do not believe is in tune with modern times.
I am as concerned about the separatist movement as anybody in the House of Commons. I was concerned on Friday or Saturday night, I forget which, when the C.B.C. national news found it necessary to take perhaps five minutes to devote to Mr. Gregoire speaking from Paris, as he explained his fund raising mission for the separatists, and how he was going to name the five or six other members of the House of Commons who endorsed his movement. I feel this was a mistake in judgment. I had more irate calls as a result of that program than any other program in months. Such a program tends to confuse the issue, tends to distort the strength of the separatist movement and tends to attract to the separatist movement what I like to call the lunatic fringe. I refer to those people who endorse a movement for the sake of publicity which, all too frequently, the C.B.C. and Radio Canada seem prone to put at their disposal.
There is something very fundamental here, and that is we cannot eradicate separatism simply by pretending it does not exist. Modern television has a duty to show separatist demonstrations when they occur. It also has
[Mr. Mackasey.l
a duty to show anti-separatist manifestations as well. Recent coverage of separatist activities in Pierrefonds, intentionally or unintentionally distorted the real strength of the outburst. have waited until now, Mr. Speaker, before entering this debate on the proposed new broadcasting legislation, because I have been trying to decide according to my own conscience what it is that I really want to say. It has been no easy assignment and I am not sure even now that I have all my thoughts straight. The job has been complicated by the fact that we are not confronted simply, as we had expected, with a bill pertaining to broadcasting; we are not challenged simply to debate upon, and deliberate upon, a legislative proposal.
Study of legislation as wide reaching and important as this, having to do with the reform and overhaul of a field as vital as broadcasting, would tax the energies of members of parliament at any time. It would constitute a heavy challenge in itself, given the happiest of circumstances. How much more difficult is the challenge this week, in a set of circumstances which are anything but happy.
I refer to the controversy currently boiling in connection with the remarks made a few days ago about the state of management within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. These remarks were by the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), the minister responsible for the bill currently before us, and the minister through whom the C.B.C. reports to parliament and the Canadian people.
The controversy which has arisen over those remarks seems now to have overshadowed the bill itself in its legislative aspects. It is already affecting the attitudes and positions of a great many members of this chamber-perhaps the majority of them-and I believe it has coloured their approach both to the basic problems afflicting broadcasting in this country and to the proposed solutions offered in the bill before us.
In my opinion this is extremely unfortunate for parliament, for all those thousands of people in Canada who are engaged in the broadcasting industry as a means of livelihood and for all those millions of Canadians who enjoy the habit of watching their television sets and listening to their radios.
For some years now, broadcasters, viewers and listeners in every comer of Canada have been waiting with the keenest of interest for new broadcasting legislation which would make the industry better fitted to inform, unite and entertain Canadians in the 20th century. Now that it is here, at least in proposal form, and ready for the scrutiny of

It is because of this ruptured approach to the legislation that I suggest it is difficult to know how best to contribute to the broadcasting debate-or even whether it is sensible to contribute to the debate at all. I have been pondering this question since the debate began last week. My difficulties are compounded by the fact that my views are not the same as those of many of my hon. friends on the Conservative benches. Generally speaking, I know the course of wisdom dictates that differences of view within a party should be reconciled in private and left unspoken in this chamber. But none of us in this house, in my opinion, are slaves to this convention. My own experience in the last two years has been that hon. members consider the institution of parliament and the business of the country to rank before party niceties-and so they should. It seems to me this is the way the majority of Canadians feel about it, too, and it is certainly in the best interest of Canadians to adhere to this philosophy. In any event, because of the nature of my remarks, and in the climate of controversy generated around the minister in the last few days I do not think it would be conscionable of me to settle my difference of opinion in private. In any case I feel it would accomplish nothing, and although it pains me to differ from some of my hon. friends I feel conscience bound to do so.
As I said earlier, I believe it is a great misfortune for the Canadian public at large that we should perhaps be allowing ourselves to become unduly influenced in our approach to highly important and long awaited public business by a peripheral and incidental matter, this matter being the controversy in which the minister has found herself embroiled. subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY

In the controversy which has arisen, it seems to me the Secretary of State has been done an injustice. Her choice of words may not have been perfect. Perhaps she should have chosen some adjective other than "rotten". Perhaps in view of the fact that a long awaited bill was coming before this chamber she should not have chosen that particular week to make the statement she did. But acknowledging this human indiscretion it appears to me patently unjust to seek to suggest that the minister's remarks were any stronger than they really were. There was nothing bombastic about the statement she made, nothing declamatory; she did not say, as some of her critics have implied, that C.B.C. management as an entity was rotten. It was not a carte blanche indictment or, in this case, a carte noire indictment. She said in the course of a lively and entertaining television interview that she thought there was some rotten management in the C.B.C., and in saying this I suspect she was speaking for many members of this party and for a great many Canadians. It is unjust to accuse her of having said more than that.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
What is more, I submit it is potentially dangerous to hound and pillory a minister for speaking out forthrightly and frankly, and for calling the shots as she or he sees them. If we persist in this kind of exercise in persecution we may come to the point where we cannot get any minister of the crown in future to answer anything. We shall moralize ourselves in our puritanical impotence right out of real life and into antiseptic neutralism.
I think perhaps the minister made a mistake. It is quite possible that if she had to do it over again she would do it differently, or perhaps not at all. But certainly one of the least attractive aspects of parliamentary life is the sometimes urge to parliamentary lynchings, the tendency of the crowd to pounce with howls of delight upon the unfortunate, on the government benches or other benches, who has the shortsightedness and the temerity to make a mistake and then is repudiated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), or the leader of his or her party.
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State said nothing that thousands of concerned Canadians have not said long ago, many of them in high public office. Of course there is some bad management in the C.B.C. If there were not, there would not have been two royal commissions investigating it in recent years; if there were not, there would not have been a dispute over the appearance on the C.B.C.
November 7, 1967

of Adolph von Thadden; if there were not, there would not have been a dispute over the appearance of George Lincoln Rockwell; if there were not, there would not have been any dispute over the downgrading of newscaster Earl Cameron; if there were not, there would not have been any dispute over the program "This Hour Has Seven Days"; and if there were not, there would not be any Bill C-163 before us in this chamber now.
Of course there is some bad management in the C.B.C. That is what this exercise in broadcasting legislation is all about. Anyone who has watched the proliferation of C.B.C. employees, anyone who has watched the C.B.C.'s annual budget spiral up to $143 million this year, anyone who has taken the trouble to compare the methods by which a private broadcaster covers an event with the methods employed by the C.B.C., knows, Mr. Speaker-he knows-that there is some bad management in the C.B.C.
The culprit in this case is not the Secretary of State. It is not even the president of the C.B.C., Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, who has one of the most difficult and thankless jobs in this country. Remember Mr. Ouimet in May of 1966 during the "Seven Days" dispute, when management's right to manage was being challenged by a group of producers, including one who has since announced his intention of becoming the first N.D.P. prime minister of Canada.
Some in this chamber who were much opposed to Mr. Ouimet in those stormy days, much in opposition to the management of the C.B.C. and in favour of the position of the producers of "Seven Days", seem now to be embracing the management people, in outrage at the remarks of the Secretary of State -a rather sharp shift in position, there, in the space of 18 months. All I would say on this point, sir, is: Where were they when management needed them?
Mr. Speaker, the culprit in this whole broadcasting crisis is not the Secretary of State, not the president of the C.B.C., but the Prime Minister of this country. He has dallied for four years with the monolith of C.B.C. problems. He has substituted wishful thinking for action. He has created Mr. Oui-met's problems for him by acquiescing in a process that year after year has squeezed control of the C.B.C. out of the president's office and diffused it among a vast army of subordinates.
The Prime Minister has constructed the Secretary of State's problem for her, by idling and fiddling, where the C.B.C. was

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting concerned, throughout the minister's stewardship in her present office. And for the finishing touch, he has repudiated her in her present difficulties by trying to suggest, in effect, that she is wrong. That's some record, Mr. Speaker.
Further, this takes no account of the frustrating and demoralizing effect on C.B.C. staffers themselves of the Prime Minister's indecisiveness. This concept in itself staggers the imagination. Imagine the position of hard working C.B.C. staffers, and there are indeed many of them, who are operating in that wasteland, in that vacuum, with no direction, no mandate, no leadership, and no stewardship worthy of the name because of the indecision of the chief legislative executive officer of this country. So the culprit in the present situation I suggest is the Prime Minister, and there is no honesty and no legitimacy in looking any further.
As to the state of broadcasting in Canada, and Bill C-163, I intend, Mr. Speaker, to reserve many of my remarks for the committee stage. But I do want to say one or two things about the present climate surrounding the situation here in the house in which we are examining this bill. There are also one or two things I wish to say about the state of broadcasting, in the few moments remaining to me on the clock at this point.
I think the C.B.C. does some very good things. Of the 265 members in the House of Commons I am among those who have been critical of the C.B.C., outspokenly critical. However I do not speak my criticism from the preferred position or the vested interest of a person who was once connected with the private broadcasting industry. I mean that sincerely, Mr. Speaker. My approach to the C.B.C., to the things it is doing, to the things it is trying to do, and to the things it fails to do is predicated purely on my love of Canada and my patriotism such as it is,-and I hope it is strong-for my country.
My partial background as a private broadcaster has nothing to do with the opinions, attitudes and positions I bring to focus on the C.B.C. in its day to day operations in this country. I hold no brief for the private broadcasters. I think private broadcasters in this country by and large-I should mention that here I speak mainly of television rather than radio-have been badly and sorely derelict in their duties to Canadian society as a whole. In most instances in which I am familiar with their operations I think they have tended to put pure business ambitions ahead of the responsibility that surely they
November 7, 1967

encourage the development of native Canadian creative performing talent. I believe that broadcasters, both public and private, tend to take the line of least resistance in all too many instances where the use of creative Canadian talent is concerned in respect of their programming. There is not enough interest in or emphasis on the development of and use of Canadian talent. I found many things in the ACTRA brief which I consider to be overstated. I even found some which I believe are partially incorrect. But in essence I agree with the appeal which is contained in the brief for a more strict and conscionable attention to the development of Canadian talent. The one medium in this country which is admirably equipped to stimulate our native creative talent and provide a showcase, a forum and a livelihood for our native Canadian performers is our broadcasting system. It does very little in this regard. I suggest that the new legislation is neither clear enough nor strong enough on that subject.
I am also somewhat dismayed by the prescription in the bill for a fine of $100,000 for certain violations of the provisions contained therein. I think that in some instances this would be a very onerous penalty, which possibly could result in the financial ruin of offending stations. I would submit that some attention could be given to the creation of a scale of fines which would provide for a less onerous burden than an arbitrary and mandatory penalty of that magnitude. In her remarks the minister implied that the wealthier a station is, the more Canadian programming will be required under the new legislation. Also implicit in that suggestion of course is the converse; that is, the poorer a station is, the less Canadian programming it will be required to do. I think this raises a question which is fraught with potential dangers for the industry and the public at large.
I ask, sir, in this connection: Who will determine whether such and such a station is wealthy enough to be required to maintain a certain degree of Canadian programming; who will determine whether some other station is not wealthy enough, or is poor enough to be allowed to get by with a minimum of Canadian programming and coast along on imported programming which does not carry with it the cost of the actual production operation?

[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
And with my Progressive Conservative friends from Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) and Winnipeg South (Mr. Sherman) coming to the defence of the Secretary of State (Miss La-Marsh), this debate is getting a bit mixed up.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext: You are mixed up all the time.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, this debate has wandered considerably from the course it took when the bill was first introduced last Wednesday. On that day, and for a short while thereafter, the house discussed the general principles of broadcasting and the general policy proposed in the legislation. It looked as though the debate might not last long and that we might get the bill to the committee at an early date.
This afternoon the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), and tonight the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) echoed his sentiments, urged that we get this part of the debate over and get the bill to committee so it can be studied in its various details. I agree with this suggestion, but I would point out that if the debate had not been muddied by certain statements, made initially outside the house by the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), it probably would have been over by last Friday. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, we have had moved today an amendment presented by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon) and it becomes necessary for the various groups in this house to indicate where they stand with respect to the amendment.
I want to make it clear that the members of this party will not support the amendment. We feel, rather, that it should be rejected and that the bill itself should be sent to the committee at the earliest possible moment. My hon. friends in the Progressive
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Conservative party, joined of course by many Liberals, have been attacking the C.B.C., today in particular, almost without mercy. But I suggest that merely because one can find fault with the C.B.C.-and all of us can do that-is no reason to pack it up. There are faults that can be pointed out in the institution of parliament. Parliament has always had its faults, and so long as they send human beings to it, it probably always will. But that is no reason for throwing out the institution of parliament itself.
I believe it is a dangerous suggestion that is being made, namely that the answer to the problems of the C.B.C. is to abolish it altogether, to sell it to private enterprise or for us to get out of this field in so far as public activity is concerned.
The proposal to deny the bill second reading at this point and to send merely its subject matter to committee would have a negative effect which we cannot accept. I may say, on the other hand, that it has no positive value that seems worth anything at all. The negative side of this amendment is that, to say the least, it delays consideration of the bill. To say the most, it kills the bill at this stage, probably for this session. All that would be referred to the committee would be its subject matter. There would be no bill, it having been denied second reading.
To do that would be to negate the proposed broadcasting policy which is set out in the bill, and in its general lines we support that policy. Therefore we cannot vote for an amendment that would negate that policy. To negate this bill by denying it second reading would also have the effect of supporting the proposition that there should not be a C.B.C., because the bill re-incorporates the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That, too, is a proposition that we cannot support. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we shall register our vote against an amendment which would have these negative and deleterious effects.
The argument has been advanced that because of the statements made last week by the Secretary of State, and the amendments and additions she has made to those statements since that time, there needs to be a committee discussion not only of the bill that is before us but of broadcasting policy and broadcasting practice in this country.
We agree that the need for this has been brought on, but there is no discussion that could be had by reference of the subject matter to the committee that cannot be had by the reference of the bill itself. The bill includes in it clauses that lay down general
November 7, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting broadcasting policy, clauses that continue a regulatory body although under a different name, and clauses that continue the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Everything that might be discussed under the heading of subject matter can be discussed by the reference of the bill itself, and we think that is what should be done.
It seems to me that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent does reflect a good many of the speeches that have been made today, such as the speech of the hon. member who moved the motion, the speech of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), the speech of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) and the speech, in large part, of the hon. member for Athabasca, even though he did come to the defence of the Secretary of State.
But it is precisely because the amendment does reflect the feeling that we should pull away from public broadcasting, that we should pull away from a public broadcasting corporation, that we feel it is not to be supported by those who have the best interests of this country at heart. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when the time comes for the vote on the amendment to the motion, we shall vote against it; and we shall vote for the second reading of the bill, welcoming of course the fact that the bill, after it has been given second reading, will be sent to the committee for thorough study.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member answer a question?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suggest to my hon. friend and neighbour from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) that there are some very distinct differences between the situation then and the situation now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY

My hon. friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) wants to know why. Naturally, I am about to explain the differences. In the case of the transportation bill

the government had come to the realization that it was not going to get it through that session, and the government itself was willing for the subject matter to be studied by the committee of the house. When the reference of the subject matter was made, and it was made unanimously, it was with the clear understanding and realization that this was the end of the bill for that session. This was a case where there had not been, in recent years at any rate, a committee study of transportation and it was desirable to have that study before the legislation was proceeded with. This was agreed to on all sides of the house. The result was of course that no legislation was passed that session but another bill had to be brought in at a subsequent session.
In the present case the whole question of broadcasting policy has already been before the committee. It got to the committee because of the "Seven Days" trouble and a few other things like that. But there has been that study, a study of the white paper, and a report from the committee recommending the general lines of broadcasting policy. This bill, therefore, is in a sense the government's answer to the consideration the committee has given to the subject matter, just as the second transportation bill was the government's answer to the study that was given to the subject matter of the first bill. Therefore I do not think the cases are parallel.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I might go one step further and say that if the course followed with respect to the transportation bill were repeated, the result would probably be the same and no broadcasting legislation would be passed in this session. If there is one thing on which we are surely agreed in the house, it is that we do not want this mess to continue ad infinitum. The time to get legislation passed with respect to broadcasting and the time to establish a regulatory body and a re-organized C.B.C. is now, not in the next session. I suggest to my friend and neighbour from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) that he has actually supported the case against the amendment, by helping me to point out that it would have this delaying effect.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Why does the hon. member think that if the bill is passed in this session anything will be done? The Prime Minister has taken well over a year to consider the resignation and to fill the position of the head of the C.B.C. and he has done
November 7, 1967

nothing about it. What makes the hon. member think the Prime Minister will be much more active next month than he has been the whole of the past year?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
That question is of course more difficult to answer, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre realizes, but let me point out to him that if the bill is not passed, then of course there is no chance of the Prime Minister doing anything. But if the bill is passed, at least it will be possible for him to act, and we would be able to goad him into action on this matter.
A good deal of the time of the debate today has been spent in attacking the C.B.C. I am prepared to admit with anyone else that the C.B.C. makes mistakes. I will assert that there are improvements in its programming and its organization that ought to be made. I am only echoing what is contained in the various reports that have been made as a result of the inquiries and the investigations that have taken place. But I suggest, even at the risk of being a small minority voice going against the stream in this chamber today, that the C.B.C. is not all that bad, and that we would be making a mistake, as I said earlier, if because of its errors and because of the things we see wrong with it, we were to destroy the institution instead of trying to reform it. That is what most of those who have spoken today offer as a solution to the problem.
I would point out to my hon. friends that we are living in the 1960's, not in the nineteenth century. There are problems facing Canadians who are alive today. Some of these problems are very real and agonizing, particularly those in the field of religious and philosophical thinking, in the field of economics, and in the whole area of the mores of our society, and the judgments that have to be made. I would suggest that in the 1960's in Canada there is one problem to which we cannot close our eyes, that is the problem of national unity which breaks down into its details, difficult though they may be, of French speaking and English speaking relationships. There are problems in the international field and in the field of race relations in the United States and in other parts of the world. I contend that any body, particularly in a field such as broadcasting, which is going to be serving the people who pay for that institution should be stimulating our thoughts and should be giving us things to think about in respect of these areas. It is no use saying that, because
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the C.B.C. goes into some of the problems related to the mores of our society, it is peddling filth or pornography, and that sort of thing. I can make the obvious retort to some of the charges that have been made, but the point I want to make is that the C.B.C., in spite of all the mistakes it has made, has been trying to cope with the problems of the human beings who are alive in 1967, and I am glad it does not pay too much attention to these voices that want to take it back into the last century.
If I had my way I would go further than this bill does so far as the C.B.C. policy is concerned. I would go more in the direction that is followed in the United Kingdom. I would say, let us set up responsible boards and a responsible management and let us pick the best people we can possibly find for the job. I may not concur in the nominations made by my friend from Winnipeg South, (Mr. Sherman).

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext: I hope not.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
I say "hear hear" to my friend who says he hopes not. I will not make my own nomination because I do not want to hurt anybody's chances, but having picked a board and having picked a management we should then give them the job. We should lay down policy, as this bill seeks to do, but then we should not interfere in the day to day operations of that body which will run the C.B.C. for us. If it lets us down, if it goes contrary to the policies that we lay down, that we think, in the name of the people of Canada, should be followed, our job is to fire them-not to carry on this business of interfering on a day to day or week to week basis of which we have had far too much in the House of Commons.
Even after all the criticisms of the C.B.C. have been made, it seems to me that on balance it has to be admitted that it has been one of the very good influences in Canadian life. It has helped to develop the consciousness of our Canadian identity. Its coverage of national events of all kinds has been outstanding. I think it has done a good deal toward Canadian unity, and I suggest we can be proud of what this organization has done.
I say again that I hope the new management will listen more to some of its creative people and will listen more to some of the suggestions that have been made. I think improvements can be made in its financial management.
November 7, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
But these criticisms have been made by others. My point is that I think something should be said on the other side. With respect to the whole question of finances I thought there was one interesting point that was brought up this afternoon which exemplies the misinformation we often get. The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) made the comparison, as other hon. members have done, between what the C.B.C. spent and what the C.T.V. spent on giving the nation the story of the Tory convention in Toronto last September. A number of figures were given. I think the figure for the C.B.C. cost has been pretty well established at $46,000. I have heard figures for the C.T.V. cost varying all the way from $12,000 to $43,000. I do not know just how we get the exact figure from the private people, the way we can get it from the public body, but I would point out that C.T.V. operated one network only, an English speaking T.V. network. The costs of the C.B.C. covered an English speaking television network, a French speaking television network, an English speaking radio network and a French speaking radio network. When one compares what was done over four networks with what was done over one network, he realizes there is room for considerable difference in the cost, and on that basis probably the C.B.C.'s cost was not as uneconomic as some people have tried to make it.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he recall that in that broadcast when people spoke in French during the convention the C.B.C. could not even find somebody to interpret? Does he remember that incident?

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY

In other words my hon. friend is complaining because on the English network French speeches were not given in English? He and I can go back to St. Jean next summer and thrash this out.
I know that these comparisons between private and public broadcasting can be made according to one's background, one's emotional reactions or one's prejudice, if you want to call it that. But it is certainly my view that had the public broadcasting in this

country not provided a stimulus the private people would not have done as good a job as some hon. members say they have done, and I think it is interesting to note that even in the United States, that great citadel of private enterprise, they are now considering the need of having a public broadcasting network.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that I thought this debate could have been ended by last Friday, and certainly by Monday at the latest, if we had stayed with the discussion of broadcasting principles and broadcasting policies which are involved in the bill. However, I suggested that we got away from that because the waters were muddied by the statements made, first outside of this house but later right here, by the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh). I want to express my very real regret that she made the statement that she did about the so-called rotten management in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In particular, I echo the views that have been expressed by my leader and deputy leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), about the responsibility of the Secretary of State and of the government in this regard. If she or the government knew in the past, or lately have become aware, that things are as bad as she makes out, they have a responsibility to do something about it rather than indulge in these general smears, on television or in the House of Commons.
I want to say that I think this is a most unfair way in which to treat Mr. Ouimet, the retiring president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. He needs no defence from me. He has been recognized as a man of brilliance and of courage. He himself has recognized that, perchance, he made some mistakes in the operation of his office. He brought that recognition to the fore by offering his resignation to the Prime Minister of this country about 13 months ago. Why is Mr. Ouimet still president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? He is still president because the Prime Minister asked him to continue until this legislation was passed, until a new president could be appointed. In other words, Mr. Ouimet's resignation is sitting on the Prime Minister's desk. Mr. Ouimet is carrying on only because he has been asked to do so. I submit it is not cricket in that situation to be kicking this man around
November 7, 1967

by the kind of charges the Secretary of State has been making.
She may say that her charge is general, that it is rotten management, in general terms, she is alleging. Surely the person who has to take responsibility for things that are wrong must be the man at the top. I think it is unfair to Mr. Ouimet who has given service to the country, and I think it is unfair to the country and unfair to parliament that we have had this discussion on one of the most important matters facing society today confused by this conflict. The whole question of radio and television and the broader question of communications are terribly important. One does not need to be able to understand Marshall McLuhan to realize that the way we communicate with each other is changing our whole way of life is perhaps changing us in the process.

I said it is not necessary to understand him in order to realize that our ways of communicating with each other are changing us into a different kind of people. It is a fact that we see things on television instead of having to read about them line by line in print. We are there when war takes place, when there is a revolution and when there are riots We can go to Expo and see these displays in which there are three or four or half a dozen film portrayals going on at the same time. This is doing something to us; it is changing us. This whole medium of television, as I say, is not merely something new that has come along, that we handle the same way our grandfathers handled the printed page. This is one of the most important factors in our life today.
What we needed in a discussion of this bill was a discussion of these basic matters. What we should have in the committee to which the bill is referred is a discussion of the whole principle and philosophy of broadcasting. I regret very much it has been muddied by this kind of discussion. Personally, I think something should be done about it. I do not expect the Prime Minister to do what he could do in this situation. This being the case, I hope we will get over this muddiness as quickly as possible, and that we will defeat this amendment which would delay the decision on broadcasting policy until next session, a fate worse than death for this country.

speechtext: This sentence has got mixed up with all these interruptions. I started out to say that in the light of this situation I believe we should defeat this delaying amendment and get the bill to the committee, so the members of that committee can deal with this very important subject.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many other members in this house I was delighted when the minister announced that after second reading this bill would be referred to the standing committee on broadcasting for very careful, detailed review. I think it should go to that committee as soon as possible, and for that reason I propose to vote against the amendment now before the house.
This bill, of course, is of the utmost importance. It affects all Canadians. I believe most Canadians feel that there are many things about Canadian broadcasting which must be improved. Their concern extends both to the stations operated by private business and to stations operated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. One of the aspects of public broadcasting, Mr. Speaker, which is causing concern to many Canadians today is the very large expense for the Canadian public broadcasting service. The C.B.C., of course, does obtain some revenue from commercial advertising, but its costs far exceed those revenues. Accordingly, during the last five years the taxpayers of Canada were called upon to pay very large amounts to the C.B.C.
I have studied the financial statements of the C.B.C. They are rather complicated, but I
November 7, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting believe my figures are approximately correct. These statistics indicate that the C.B.C.'s financial year ends on March 31, and that for the financial year ending March 31, 1964, the Canadian taxpayers were forced to pay C.B.C. operating costs amounting to $78.4 million and capital costs amounting to $7.3 million, for a total of $85.7 million. In 1965 the operating deficit of the C.B.C. amounted to $85.8 million, while capital costs amounted to $14.2 million, for a total cost of $100 million. This $14.2 million was in the form of a loan, but it was never paid back. So in effect it was another grant from public revenues. In 1966, the operating deficit of the C.B.C. amounted to $94.3 million, and capital costs were $12.5 million, making a total of $106.8 million. In 1967, operating deficits amounted to $112.4 million, while capital costs were $29 million for a total of $141.4 million.
The question in my mind is simply this: Are the Canadian people getting full value for these tax dollars? If not, will the present bill deal adequately with the problem?
If I may turn for a moment to the private stations in Canada, it appears that they constitute a system of about the same size as the C.B.C. In the early years some of these stations were unprofitable. However, in recent years private business has been able to operate both radio and television stations at a profit. Accordingly, instead of being subsidized by the taxpayers, they have contributed a substantial amount to the public treasury through taxes on their profits.
During the entire history of radio and television broadcasting in Canada, one of the most difficult, controversial and time consuming jobs of the public regulating authority has been the issuing of licences to private stations. At times there has been great competition for these licences, perhaps stimulated by the well known remark that a broadcasting licence is a licence to print money, unless it is issued to the C.B.C. I am not sure that this statement is true, but it may be true to some extent.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Accordingly, I hope that the Secretary of State will, during the course of discussion in committee, consider an amendment which will require broadcasting licences, and licences which are to be renewed, to be issued on the basis of public tender. If the owner of a private station bids too low and fails to renew his licence, the physical assets of his station would be transferred to the

successful bidder at fair book value, determined in accordance with the regulations of the broadcasting commission. This system would remove all suspicion of favouritism and would provide the government with revenue. I hope the minister is sympathetic to the suggestion.
Turning for a moment to the C.B.C., because the corporation forms almost half our broadcasting system we cannot make any sensible decisions with regard to broadcasting legislation until we make some basic decisions with regard to the functions and physical structure of the C.B.C.
The Fowler committee made this fundamental point very clearly when it said at page 81 of its report:
It is extremely important that government policy should clearly determine the physical structure of the C.B.C. system for at least the next five years. This is an essential first step. Upon this decision a great many others depend.
The present physical structure of the C.B.C. has developed over a long period of time and now needs very careful re-examination. When the C.B.C. was formed many years ago for radio broadcasting, means of communication were primitive by present day standards. Great stretches of the country were not equipped with broadcasting facilities. The large amounts of capital required were not readily available. The government owned network financed by Canadian taxpayers was the only practical way of bringing news, entertainment and cultural programs to many parts of our country.
In response to this need the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was formed and gradually acquired stations and physical facilities, until in 1965 the facilities owned by the C.B.C. included 16 television stations with 28 relays, 31 AM stations with 129 relays, and 5 FM radio stations. In addition, of course, it had arrangements for its programs to be carried by its affiliated stations throughout the country.
In recent years conditions have changed radically; the heavily populated parts of Canada are all served by numerous privately owned radio and T.V. stations and most Canadians are subject to an almost overwhelming bombardment of light entertainment, news, public affairs, and cultural programs from many different sources. Nevertheless, despite these radical changes, the
November 7, 1967

C.B.C. has continued to insist that it must increase the number of its stations and extend and expand its physical facilities at the cost of the taxpayers. This is referred to in the Fowler report at page 78:
The current C.B.C. five year forecast of capital and operating requirements includes provision for a very substantial extension of coverage that does not commend itself to us.
The committee then quotes from a document entitled "General Coverage Policy- October, 1964" which reads as follows:
In television, in AM radio and in FM radio, the long range goal of the corporation as the national service has been to eventually provide all Canadians with C.B.C. program services in full.
It then outlines the necessity for additional facilities and says:
A less tangible but most important factor is the need for a C.B.C. "presence" in all parts of the country.
The document concludes with these words:
Consequently, in the light of the three foregoing factors:
(1)	the need to bring the complete C.B.C. service to all Canadians,
(2)	the desire of the public for truly alternative service, and
(3)	the need for a C.B.C. "presence" across the country as an essential factor in developing Canadian unity,
the C.B.C. believes it is in the best public interest to follow a policy under which its program services will ultimately be broadcast in full and to all Canadians through C.B.C.-owned facilities.
If this policy were carried out it would involve an extensive expansion of existing C.B.C. facilities at great expense to the Canadian treasury. That is the policy which did not commend itself to the Fowler committee. That committee had this to say in that regard:
To ensure satisfactory distribution of the national service some minor changes in the arrangements with the affiliates may be necessary. But there is no valid reason for further expansion of C.B.C. production and transmission facilities. Any additional public money provided to the C.B.C. would be much better spent on improvement of its programming.
The ACTRA brief which most members of parliament received recently made the same points, with the additional suggestion that the money should be spent on Canadian rather then United States programming.
This raises a very fundamental question. Under present conditions is it necessary for the C.B.C. to own and operate its stations and physical facilities? Would it not be more
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting efficient if licences for all stations were allotted by public tender and if there were reserved for the C.B.C. generous amounts of time on all the Canadian stations for it to present its programs. Broadcasting time should be so arranged that worth-while national broadcasts can be adequately presented in a proper and adequate manner across the nation. Time reservations could be arranged so that people in practically all populated areas would have a choice. They could watch either the national broadcasting service provided by the C.B.C. or private programs.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
The Fowler committee considered this suggestion but rejected it. At page 80 of its report, referring to the C.B.C., it says this:
First, it must have a basic number of stations that it owns and operates. To be an effective broadcasting agency, the C.B.C. must have continuing experience in actual broadcasting and maintain direct contact with the viewing and listening public. If the C.B.C. were ever to become a mere producer of programs available for transmission over stations controlled and operated by others, it would lose contact with the needs and tastes of the Canadian people, and its programs would soon lose the character of a vital national service. The C.B.C. now owns 16 television stations and 36 AM and FM radio stations. These, we believe, are quite sufficient to give it experience and direct participation in actual broadcasting.
I have read that statement a number of times. I find it difficult to assess its validity because no reasons are given for it. It seems completely inconsistent with the much quoted sentence with which the report begins:
The only thing that really matters in broadcasting is program content; all the rest is housekeeping.
Did the Fowler committee really mean that, or did it put that sentence in merely as a controversial opening sentence for an interesting report?
If generous amounts of time are reserved on stations throughout the nation so that an appropriate network is required to be provided for the national broadcasting service, why should it be essential that the C.B.C. should have legal title to the stations and physical facilities and actually carry out the housekeeping operations.
Personally, I feel that our firm in Toronto can work satisfactorily and carry on a satisfactory practice without owing the Toronto-Dominion Centre in which we reserve office
November 7, 1967

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting space. Had we access to the treasury we might And it desirable to own the building; since we have not, we are willing to go along as we are. Many professional and businessmen are quite satisfied to work in office space that is reserved for them in buildings owned by others. It is not necessary for them to own the buildings in which they work. Housekeeping facilities must be provided efficiently, but they do not need to be operated by the business or professional firms which use them.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The same principle surely applies to the C.B.C. All our experience in Canada indicates that housekeeping operations connected with the functioning of broadcasting stations could be provided much more efficiently and economically by private operators rather than by organizations such as the C.B.C. which rely on subsidies from the public treasury.
The Fowler report gives many examples of the inefficiency of the C.B.C. when carrying out these housekeeping operations. Referring to the proposed new C.B.C. building in Montreal, the report says at page 205:
Work measurement tests indicate that for both administrative and operational or production processes there is a need for the development and implementation of precise standards, from which one could reasonably anticipate staff savings of up to 20 per cent of the present totals in these classes of employment. C.B.C. management does not agree with this estimate. However, obstinate disbelief in the validity of work measurement techniques is an anachronism today; we must therefore assume that future growth could be modified by savings from increased efficiency in the future, and it could well be that the planned staff increase in Montreal need not be anticipated in the building program.
Speaking of the proposed new buildings both in Montreal and Toronto, the report said, at page 209:
We must emphasize that our analysis clearly confirms the need for immediate relief, both in Montreal and Toronto. We are equally sure that existing C.B.C. plans for rectifying this situation are not well founded. In our view, they take insufficient account of new and prospective developments and trends, both in programming and electronics, and are consequently too extravagant and inflexible. We are satisfied that they should be reviewed ab initio, and redesigned in accordance with the principles we have advanced above.
At page 263, in the same vein, the Fowler report has this to say, speaking of the changes which might come about as the result of the possible use of satellites, laser

beams and other technological improvements in communications:
For broadcasting policy, the bearings are obvious. In developing the Canadian national broadcasting system, great care must be taken not to hinder tomorrow's advance by vast investments in facilities and equipment that belong to yesterday's technology. There must be elbow room to take advantage of each scientific discovery as it becomes available for practical purposes. New and better ways of producing and transmitting broadcast programs must not be baulked by costly but outdated buildings that will remain only as durable monuments to lack of foresight. We have all seen such monuments in our travels, some of then not far from home.
At page 298, speaking of C.B.C. administration, the report says:
Some 1,500 to 1,600 C.B.C. personnel have clerical and supervisory duties, with annual salaries totalling $7,500,000. The study indicates a potential saving of $900,000 to $1,200,000 or 12 per cent to 16 per cent.
I believe it is a fundamental mistake to assume that these inefficiencies can be changed for long merely by bringing about a change in management. I say this although I very seldom disagree with my hon. friend from Verdun (Mr. Mackasey). The simple fact is, our experience has shown that over a long period of time housekeeping operations of this type are not carried out efficiently by any government, any public corporation or any commission which relies largely upon public subsidies.
The private operation of such facilities has built-in safeguards against operational inefficiency and waste of money, and we should take advantage of this principle. Accordingly when the bill before us goes to committee I hope the minister will be prepared to accept amendments along the lines I have suggested.
To continue to deal with the subject of efficiency, let me draw attention to the fact that the present bill contemplates the head office of the corporation remaining in Ottawa. The Fowler report clearly documented the inefficiency of keeping a large head office staff in Ottawa, remote from the two large operational centres in Toronto and Montreal, and recommended that the head office be removed to one of the operating centres, preferably Montreal.
It is surely entirely clear to all that there is no point whatever in continuing to maintain at great expense a large head office staff at the Ottawa headquarters on Bronson avenue. I suggest that the formal, statutory head office should remain in Ottawa at the office of
November 7, 1967

the Secretary of State, but that no executive staff should be there; the executive headquarters would be removed to Toronto or Montreal. In any event the top executive staff would be obliged to move between those two centres. In this way, very substantial sums of money would be saved and operational efficiency would be increased. No doubt the expensive monument on Bronson avenue could be used by one of the other government departments and large amounts saved by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) !or his economy program.
I have suggested that licences for all stations should be granted by public tender to qualified persons, and that adequate time for the national broadcasting service should be reserved to the C.B.C. at such time as licences are issued. It is not necessary for the C.B.C. to own its stations and physical facilities. In addition to the savings which would be effected in the operation of these facilities there would also be substantial savings in program costs.
It is important that there should be available to Canadians a balanced program including news, public affairs, light entertainment and cultural and educational programs, but it is not necessary that the C.B.C. should at the expense of the taxpayers duplicate the light entertainment, the news and the public affairs programs now being provided adequately by private stations in most parts of Canada. Nevertheless, a very large proportion of the present C.B.C. budget is spent in duplicating services already provided without expense to the taxpayer by private broadcasters.

CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST FOR CONTINUATION OF SERVICE IN LOWER ST. LAWRENCE REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 19 last, I asked the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), if his department anticipated the replacement of the Ocean Limited train which was supposed to be cancelled on October 29 and which has acutally been cancelled since.
I directed the question to the hon. minister at that time because I considered the matter as very urgent. As a matter of fact, the people of my constituency and the whole district are greatly concerned about this situation which is not only getting worse but which has been deteriorating for many years without any remedial action being taken.
A few days before putting this question, I received a copy of the daily editorial of station CJBR, Rimouski. At the very outset of this broadcast appeared these words I wish to quote on the cancellation of this train.
Such is the absolutely staggering news made public by the Canadian National. The inadequate, insufficient and unfair service of which the population has been complaining for years, particularly since the opening of Expo, far from improving, is deteriorating.
And the editorial writer added:
-we can no longer have any doubt that the C.N.R. is discriminating against the population of eastern Quebec.
November 7, 1967
4024	COMMONS DEBATES
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The editorial writer gave proof, brought out facts to support the opinions he expressed. For instance, he mentioned the problems of seat, berth, and compartment reservations on trains in our area when we want to go to the provincial capital or to Montreal.
He gave this recent example:
Last Monday evening, on Thanksgiving day, the 11.15 p.m. train which had been booked up for a week, according to the Campbellton office, had only 74 passengers out of a 300-seat capacity.
It is things like this which have for years prompted the people in our area to criticize and to feel left out. The announcement that that train was to be cancelled certainly did not soothe or encourage them.
At about the same time, the Progres du golfe on October 26, published an editorial entitled:
In the age of cybernetics, service of another age.
The editorial writer recognizes the qualities of this crown corporation, the Canadian National. She praises its achievements of recent years; she praises also the part played by the Canadian National in the success of our Expo, but in concluding, she raises the same questions and shares the opinion I have already expressed, when she says:
If only there were trains-
She says that because people speak of improvements in transportation, in cybernetics, in electronics, in transportation with powerful diesel engines. But if only there were trains. I continue:
We had so few; we will have fewer still. What can we do, except maintain and even prove by scores of testimonies that C.N. users in the Lower St. Lawrence are the most disadvantaged of all passengers. The time of Expo 67-
That is from the standpoint of transportation.
-was not easy for them but the prospects after Expo (in the field of transportation) do not look much brighter. It is not the C.N.R. which is lagging behind, but its passengers.
I have received since then from the municipal councils of Rimouski, Saint-Fabien and other localities, resolutions which express the same views.
That is why I deemed it advisable to make representations to the new minister who, I believe, will enunciate, through his parliamentary secretary, the position he intends to take so as to meet the demands of the people of that pilot area, about which we have been

hearing throughout the country for some years in the field of railway transportation.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-GEORGIAN BAY-CONSIDERATION UNDER DESIGNATED AREA PROGRAM
INDUSTRY-GEORGIAN BAY-CONSIDERATION UNDER DESIGNATED AREA PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 1, 1967, as reported at page 3741 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) this question:
In view of the fact that the removal of the southern Georgian Bay region from the list of designated areas discriminates against the Owen Sound area, which now has close to 2,100 men and women seeking employment there, will he give consideration to restoring this region to the list of designated areas or to making special provision for the Owen Sound employment area?
The minister did not answer. Tonight, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on the record the reason I feel Owen Sound and Meaford have received unjust and shabby treatment from the Minister of Industry.
November 7, 1967

When the designation legislation became effective and the regions were being designated, this government which was well aware of our plight, ignored the fact that the Georgian bay area has been long recognized as a slow growth area with hundreds of unemployed, with hundreds of marginal farms, with thousands of people struggling on inadequate incomes and with a continuing migration of the youth and high school graduates to more prosperous centres. After ignoring these facts the government then selected certain other areas, some of which already were highly industrialized, for designation benefits.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The Georgian bay area was actually penalized for two years while the cream of new industry was attracted to areas under designation. Eventually, after many appeals for consideration over a two year period, the Georgian bay area was designated. However, owing to an ill-conceived formula, most of the available industry coming to this area located at the nearest possible point to the potential market to the south, resulting in the large majority of the industry locating in two centres. Out of the 68 industries reported to have received development benefits in the Georgian bay area, Meaford did not get any new industry; Owen Sound got four new industries, and five others received benefits for modernization. However, during this same period three industries closed their doors in Owen Sound.
Owen Sound placed much confidence in two statements made by the minister in his press release of August 5, 1965 at the time of our designation. Let me quote these excerpts as follows:
I am confident that many areas which may have been considered remote for industrial development in the past will offer most attractive opportunities for growth in the future.
The second excerpt is:
The duration of the incentive program is designed to ensure the best possible results in that the benefits will be available to eligible firms which enter production before expiry of the plan, March 31, 1971.
On the strength of these and other assurances given at that time Owen Sound began a program of essential services required by industry that might locate there, at a cost of approximately $1 million. Further evidence of the city's financial involvement is outlined in an editorial which appeared in the Owen
DEBATES	4026
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Sound Sun Times of November 3, 1967. 1 should like to quote from this editorial ai follows:
A great deal of the economy of the district has been built on indications that the assistance would continue for another two years or so. Owen Sound for instance has faced a heavy burden in its very costly water pumping station, whose extent was based on a continuing industrial expansion under the designated area status and the demands such would create. The city has built up a reserve of industrial land based on the same premise. Extensive school expansion programs have been undertaken with a view to the continued growth in population. Multi-unit housing programs are now under way. Other smaller communities in the area have yet to feel the results of the assistance program, Meaford as an instance.
Considering the comparatively small percentage of the benefits received by Owen Sound with over 18,000 population and Meaford with 3,800, one can fully realize it does not balance with the burden Owen Sound will have to bear. Not only will we suffer from the loss of our ability to attract industry, but our winter works program will require that we pay 25 per cent of the cost, while under designation we paid 10 per cent. On Owen Sound's proposed winter works program, amounting to better than $1,250,000, the extra cost to the city will be $187,500. Furthermore, thinking people for quite some time now have been alarmed at the way our most productive land is being sacrificed for industrial sites and subdivision development. In fact, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) mentioned this in a speech he made in Toronto last Saturday, November 4.
Meaford and Owen Sound are strategic locations with an abundance of land unsuitable for agriculture, and ideal municipalities for government assistance to further industrial and population growth. To deprive these centres of assistance when their development was only in the bud was the height of poor judgment. The irony of the whole matter stems from the fact that when the Owen Sound employment area qualified for designation on August 5, 1965, there were 748 people unemployed. On the same date this year we had 1,625 unemployed and we are deprived of designation benefits when the need is most urgent.
I appeal to the minister to use his influence toward restoring assistance to Meaford and Owen Sound for at least another year, so that they might get their feet on more solid ground.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: INDUSTRY-GEORGIAN BAY-CONSIDERATION UNDER DESIGNATED AREA PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having seen representatives from Owen Sound here a little over a week ago, I am afraid the hon. member and myself are operating on rather different figures. As I think you, Mr. Speaker, will be aware, the designated area program is not applied to municipalities, but rather to larger areas known as manpower service centre areas. These larger areas are chosen for designation, so as to give the prospective investor a reasonable range of choice in respect of the location of his prospective new investment.
In this region mention has been made of three manpower service centre areas, namely Midland, Owen Sound and Collingwood. Comparing these three areas, the unemployment ratio, on which basically designation is founded in relation to Canada as a whole with a national average of 100 per cent, for the most recent five years for Collingwood was 141 per cent, for Midland 135.9 per cent and for Owen Sound only 111.5 per cent. This would indicate that Owen Sound is the better off, in terms of unemployment, of the three areas.
The hon. member has mentioned that at the time of de-designation there had been approved, or the three designated areas qualified for grants in respect of some 68 projects, which incidentally represent a new investment of some $105 million. When finally brought to fruition and in production these projects will result in the creation of some 6,500 new jobs. That is for the three areas. My information is that of those 68 projects, 18 will be in Collingwood, 19 will be in Midland and 31 will be in Owen Sound.
In terms of investment value, $32,250,000 will be for Midland, $35 million will be for Collingwood and $38,400,000 will be for Owen Sound. In terms of jobs, these 68 projects will represent 1,500 new jobs for Collingwood, 2,000 new jobs for Midland and 2,876 new jobs for Owen Sound. I would think it is clear, therefore, that while one municipality, Meaford, has had no industrial expansion, the manpower service centre area of Owen Sound, which according to the hon. gentleman has had virtually no expansion, has benefited from substantial industrial expansion. A manpower service centre area is by definition an area which represents a common labour market.
As evidence perhaps of more than local success in relieving unemployment, the hon.

DEBATES	November 7, 196'1'
member has mentioned the fact that row housing projects are in the course of construction. This would indicate that new houses are needed to house additional people. Therefore the new industrial jobs would, on the face of it, appear to be not only taking care of the local unemployment situation but also making provision for new jobs for new entrants into the area.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
As I pointed out to the delegation from Owen Sound, it is not the purpose and object of this program to accelerate or indeed to induce industrial expansion in rural areas but rather to provide new job opportunities in areas of Canada, whether urban or rural, suffering from high chronic unemployment. One has been successful, and I suggest in this case the success has been more than moderate. It is clear that the incentives which accompany designation should be removed and be applied to those less favoured, less fortunate areas where chronic unemployment continues to be high and unrelieved.
